We introduce an approach to pre-training deep neural networks for semantic segmentation by utilizing depth estimation derived from unsupervised videos. Our strategy involves training a convolutional neural network for semantic segmentation through a supervised loss function, using as input both the original images and the depth maps generated by an independently trained, unsupervised video depth estimation model. Our findings indicate that this method significantly enhances performance on the Cityscapes dataset, achieving an improvement of approximately 2.5% in mIoO compared to equivalent architectures initialized with random weights, all without necessitating additional computational resources for the depth estimation step during the main training phase.

Temporal data, such as time-series, is ubiquitous in various domains, including finance, medicine, and weather forecasting. While current methods primarily generate static visualizations or interactive dashboards, this paper introduces TCube, a narrative approach designed to help users understand the statistical properties of temporal data through animated narratives. By leveraging dynamic animations, TCube conveys the statistical behavior of datasets interactively. Our primary contribution is a novel narrative structure that utilizes time-sliders to synchronize both visual and textual storytelling elements. This structure allows for the flexible arrangement of temporal animations and supporting text, enabling efficient narration of complex statistics. We have developed a viewer application for TCube that facilitates the creation of these stories via a user-friendly interface. Additionally, our experiments using both real and synthetic datasets demonstrate that TCube effectively supports data analysis and that its generated stories are highly rated for their ease of construction.

The ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has recorded proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. Analyses of these datasets address two key areas: $b$-hadron properties and $b$-hadron production dynamics. Specifically, this work reports findings on CP violation within neutral $B$ mesons and on the determination of the mixing-induced CP asymmetry in $B^0 \to D^{(*)}K^+\pi^-$ decays. Additionally, cross-section measurements are presented for $B_s^0$, $B_s^{*}$, $B_s^{+}$, $B_s^{0}$, $B_s^{+}$, $B_s^{0}$, $B_s^{+}$, $B_s^{0}$, $B_s^{+}$, $B_s^{0}$, $B_s^{+}$, $B_s^{0}$, $B_s^{+}$, $B_s^{0}$, $B_s^{+}$, $B_s^{0}$, $B_s^{+}$, $B_s^{0}$, $B_s^{+}$, $B_s^{0}$, $B_s^{+}$, $B_s^{0}$, $B_s^{+}$, $B_s^{0}$, $B_s^{+}$, $B_s^{0}$, $B_s

We investigate the Ising model within a Cayley tree context, uncovering new weakly periodic measures that align with normal subgroups of index 2 from the tree-Cayley tree's CW group.

The investigation reveals novel weakly periodic Ising model configurations on Cayley trees that correspond to normal subgroups of index two from the associated Cayley tree CW group.

This paper investigates the large-scale behavior of parameters in solutions to partially separated strictly hyperbolic equations, which possess coefficients that experience limited singularities. By integrating these findings with results from our earlier work (arXiv:2004.01532), we demonstrate the existence of a specific class of coefficients for such equations that exhibit a self-similar structure. This discovery establishes a link between the equation's solutions and a model defined by a differential equation with a focus singularity. Additionally, we establish the stability of these self-similar coefficients under perturbations.

This paper introduces a deep-learning-based Japanese word segmentation (WSS) framework that leverages segmentable contexts to address the task. Japanese presents distinct challenges compared to Chinese, primarily due to a higher rate of out-of-vocabulary (OOV) occurrences in Japanese, which deep learning models typically struggle to handle. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel OOV handling mechanism that functions by learning the probability of a phrase being segmentable given its context. This approach enables the use of multiple segmentation tools to generate various candidate phrases, allowing the model to evaluate their contextual plausibility. Experiments demonstrate that this method significantly outperforms both traditional methods and existing deep-learning approaches, achieving a precision of 99.43% on the MeCab benchmark with a precision score of 94.93% on the Kuakal benchmark.

On Stack Overflow, users can attach external links to their posts, a feature that promotes knowledge sharing but also introduces the risk of malicious content infiltration. This study examines link-sharing patterns to identify opportunities for improvement. Our analysis reveals that 82% of connections originate from external sources, with 60% of those appearing only once. Although the majority of users share links infrequently, a small group of power users accounts for the bulk of activity. The data indicates a strong correlation between a user's reputation and their sharing frequency, suggesting that occasional users are more likely to distribute potentially harmful links than established members. Our findings offer valuable insights for enhancing the link-sharing mechanisms within communities similar to Stack Overflow.

We introduce a new set of cosmological simulations incorporating Self-Interacting Dark Matter (SIDM) alongside baryonic physics, specifically designed to examine how baryonic feedback mechanisms influence the inner regions of dark matter halos. Our models utilize a free-streaming mean free path for SIDM particles and employ a novel, efficient technique to accurately map post-simulation dark matter velocity distributions. We investigate three distinct Self-Interaction Cross-section ($\sigma/m$) models—ranging from Cold Dark Matter (CDM) to one with isotropic scattering and another with anisotropic scattering—to evaluate the impact of scattering angles on the resulting halo structures. Our results indicate that SIDM models with a $\sigma/m$ of $1\,\mathrm{cm^2/g}$ successfully reproduce the observed core/cusp transition in galaxy centers, a capability that CDM models lack. Furthermore, we demonstrate that while baryonic feedback significantly alters the inner halo structure in both standard and self-interacting scenarios, the final outcomes in CDM and SIDM with anisotropic scattering remain distinguishable from those with isotropic scattering. Consequently, our findings suggest that future observations of galactic central regions can effectively constrain both the dark matter particle physics and the specific details of baryonic feedback history.

This paper investigates how to convey scientific evidence of climate change effectively, a task complicated by the complex nature of the data and the diverse backgrounds of recipients. To create more personalized communication strategies, the authors propose a new framework for profiling individuals based on their values, prior knowledge, and emotional responses regarding the climate crisis. By combining a values model with a knowledge graph, the study demonstrates an innovative method to identify suitable knowledge pathways. Additionally, the work addresses the role of hope in fostering pro-climate actions and introduces a computational method to detect hopeful language within social media posts. Collectively, these tools allow for the development of tailored messaging that maximizes both understanding of the science and engagement in climate mitigation efforts.

Although symptom extraction from electronic health records has been extensively explored, variations in clinical practices and terminology across different institutions often limit the generalizability of current models. We introduce a novel pre-training approach that leverages medical background knowledge to enhance symptom detection across diverse contexts. Extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets demonstrate that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art systems. Additionally, we release SymBERT, a pre-trained language model specifically designed for symptom detection tasks.

Autonomous driving is a highly complex multi-task system that relies on specific subroutines, such as semantic parsing, object detection, and motion prediction. Currently, these modules are typically trained independently, often resulting in suboptimal overall performance. Although joint training all components end-to-end is an attractive solution, a significant barrier remains: most real-world driving datasets contain annotations suitable only for the primary perception tasks, lacking the necessary labels for downstream tasks like motion prediction. To overcome this limitation, we introduce "drop-out motion prediction," a novel framework for collaborative multi-task training. This approach involves randomly excluding certain tasks during the training process, allowing the model to focus on those currently active while still benefiting from the structure of the full system. Our method effectively addresses the lack of global ground truth by enabling individual modules to learn jointly despite some being temporarily dropped. Experiments conducted on the challenging nuScenes dataset confirm that drop-out motion prediction significantly enhances performance across every single task within the pipeline.

Although Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) have driven significant recent breakthroughs in computer vision, they demand extensive training and inference resources due to their continuous processing nature. In contrast, Biological Neural Networks (BNNs) operate on discrete spikes, offering superior space and temporal efficiencies. Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) serve as a bridge between ANNs and BNNs, yet their potential has been limited by the lack of effective biologically plausible learning rules for complex tasks like object recognition. This paper introduces a new, biologically realistic learning algorithm for developing Object Recognition SNNs. We successfully trained an Object Recognition SNN with 100 million synapses to achieve 90.1% accuracy on the ImageNet dataset, a result that surpasses current benchmarks for deep learning approaches. Furthermore, our model demonstrates a 2.5x reduction in computational cost compared to standard deep learning methods.

The paper investigates the thermodynamic properties of spin-polarized strange quark matter under finite temperature conditions, employing the MIT bag model alongside an analytical framework for finite temperature and magnetic field effects on the bosonic and fermionic components. Using this approach, we calculate the incompressibility coefficient, Fermi energy, Fermi momentum, Fermi temperature, as well as the contributions from leptons and baryons within the MIT bag model. Our findings indicate that increasing the magnetic field results in elevated baryon chemical potential, Fermi temperature, momentum, and incompressibility coefficient, while baryon Fermi energy exhibits behavior contingent upon the specific field intensity. These computed values align with experimental observations, suggesting magnetic fields may induce the formation of strange quark matter.

This paper introduces Pando, a distributed volunteer computing framework designed to harness the idle capacity of smartphones and tablets. The system executes parallel tasks across these devices, offering a cost-free, readily available tool for parallel processing. The authors demonstrate the utility of Pando with a case study on image classification, proving its effectiveness in supporting other computational demands. The study also investigates the impact of user demographics, device specifications, and network conditions on the framework's performance. The paper concludes by outlining the study's limitations and suggesting directions for future research.

This study introduces a novel approach to addressing the nonlinear eigenvalue problem, centered on approximate solving the associated vector equation via a vectorization technique. The eigenvalues and their corresponding eigenvectors are identified by applying the MRIF method for vector interpolation, specifically targeting the rational representation of vectors derived from a vector equation dependent on the scalar parameter. The resulting eigenpairs are extracted by analyzing the roots of a scalar equation constructed through the denominator of these interpolated vectors utilizing MRIF. The eigenvalues are subsequently determined by resolving this constructed scalar equation using available numerical methods. The paper details the derivation of the rational interpolation method within the framework of the VIE problem, detailing the implementation of the proposed numerical method, validating its efficacy through examples, and illustrating its performance with results from actual experiments. The final section summarizes the paper's contributions and outlines directions for future investigation.

We demonstrate that certain intermediate $\beta$-transformations, which are non-greedy systems, can be modeled as greedy $\beta$-transformations featuring a hole at zero. Consequently, the orbit of zero exhibits a dense set of gaps, implying the transformation is locally invertible only on a subset of the domain. Furthermore, we establish the existence of an intermediate $\beta$-system that is related to the greedy $\beta$-system of the same base value. The latter possesses a dense set of gaps in its orbit for zero, confirming the system's local invertibility only locally rather than entirely. Under specific conditions, both transformations share an identical set of $\beta$-numbers. These findings rely on the construction of a novel class of parabolic continued fractions, the periods of which are dense.

We demonstrate that confinement arises from monopole condensation in $SO(N_{c})$ gauge theories featuring vectors, establishing the equivalence of these theories with those containing fermions in the vector representation through the presence of a single scalar field in the vector representation coupled to a cubic self-interaction. This interaction drives the theory to a point on its manifold of massless renormalization group fixed points. Notably, adding this scalar to a theory of fermions in the vector representation enables the system to flow from a renormalization group fixed point involving the scalar within an $SO(N_{c})$ context to another within an $Sp(N_{c})$ context, provided the matter content is adjusted appropriately.

Tree ensemble methods are widely adopted for their ability to deliver both high predictive accuracy and interpretability. However, traditional feature importance metrics often fail to capture complex relationships, such as feature interactions, when analyzing model behavior. We introduce Disentangled Attribution Curves (DAC), a novel approach that visualizes a feature's influence on predictions across a sorted dataset to produce stable and meaningful importance scores. By integrating tree structure with feature values within DAC, we demonstrate enhanced performance on both predictive tasks and attribution analysis compared to state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, we outline efficient algorithms for computing DACs in randomized ensemble models like Random Forests and demonstrate their application in analyzing feature contributions to various downstream tasks across multiple real-world datasets.

Federated learning (FL) enables the collaborative training of machine learning models across multiple devices while keeping raw data local. Nevertheless, FL is susceptible to privacy breaches via malicious inference attacks, where adversaries analyze shared model updates to deduce sensitive private information. Although various defenses exist, they are ineffective against such attacks when the communication channels between the client and server are compromised. To address this, our solution integrates Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), which provide a secure environment for computing private data operations. By utilizing TEEs, our TEE-FL framework ensures complete confidentiality of both the initial model parameters and the returned updates, rendering them unintelligible to any attacker, even those with access to the network. Furthermore, we have developed optimized, TEE-compatible algorithms that preserve the client-server communication flow. Comprehensive experiments conducted on real hardware demonstrate that our TEE-FL approach successfully prevents malicious inference attacks while incurring only a minimal performance penalty.

Embedded systems are ubiquitous in our daily lives, yet their interaction with external peripherals often complicates both the creation and verification of this critical software. These complications primarily stem from the lack of control over the physical environment, the difficulty in emulating hardware, and the inherent non-determinism associated with drivers. Consequently, the process of locating and fixing bugs is significantly slowed. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a novel, lightweight, and non-intrusive approach for automatically generating call graphs in real-time embedded systems. Our method analyzes the execution of programs to capture function call relationships, requiring no modifications to the source code, the compiler, or the running binary. The solution is designed to be cost-effective and easy to deploy, making it suitable for a wide range of applications.

We introduce Timeloops, a novel system that leverages runtime observations to generate cost-efficient filter strategies for syscall-level Application Performance Monitoring (APM). Existing solutions typically rely on either data-driven methods, which create runtime filters but incur high costs that degrade application performance, or static analysis-based techniques, which lower filter costs but struggle with the runtime variability characteristic of cloud-native microservices. Timoloops addresses these limitations by dynamically constructing filter strategies tailored to specific execution traces, thereby reducing filter costs for particular runtime instances. This approach utilizes an original method for extracting call graph information from execution without requiring static analysis, combined with graph-structured strategy generation. Additionally, Timoloops employs dynamic program slicing to adapt filter strategies in real-time by observing execution. Our evaluation across four production microservice applications demonstrates that Timoloops achieves filter costs comparable to static analysis-based approaches while drastically lowering the rate of false negative alerts compared to data-driven alternatives, all while maintaining negligible impacts on application latency or CPU usage.

We demonstrate that for any metric space $X$, the space of directed distances $\mathcal{D}(X)$—comprising pairs of points $(x,y)$ representing $(x, y)$—carries a non-positive curvature (geodesic Cayley) structure. This allows the construction of linear classifiers within $\mathcal{D}(X)$, which we prove are capable of exactly replicating the functionality of trees, even in settings where $X$ is high-dimensional. Consequently, an analysis of linear models in feature spaces of arbitrary curvature and dimension offers a robust theoretical basis for understanding the performance of ensemble methods.

This study presents a novel theoretical framework for the spatial distribution of stars in the vicinity of a galaxy's central supermassive black hole (SMBH). We propose that the stellar population near an SMBH consists of a cluster of stars that have collapsed into the black hole's gravitational well, exhibiting a power-law distribution. This model is theoretically underpinned by the principle that stellar collapse is most probable when a star's mass closely mirrors the enclosed black hole mass. Furthermore, we theorize that the stellar cluster surrounding an SMBH possesses a stellar mass equal to the black hole's mass, thereby forming what we term a "mirror black hole." Consequently, the surrounding stellar cluster effectively masks the true black hole, rendering it observationally indistinguishable from a conventional star cluster.

This short overview introduces an STMC framework focused on stochastic model predictive control with a primary aim of minimizing the statistical dispersion of the stochastic control problem. To achieve this, the study employs a novel statistical dispersion metric that relies on the covariance of statistical moments for statistical analysis. The proposed method optimizes statistical moments within a single-stage stochastic control setup, utilizing a linear thermal model to represent electrical load management. The paper demonstrates the application of this technique in a load management case study.

Compressive learning represents a promising framework for acquiring structured knowledge from data, characterized by the use of a measurement matrix to reduce the number of samples required for effective learning. Recently, there has been a growing emphasis on the data recovery stage, particularly within matrix and tensor completion problems, where Sparsity and low-rank properties are exploited to reduce complexity. In this paper, we extend these principles by introducing a novel measurement matrix designed for general learning tasks that taps into both the sparsity and structural characteristics of student models to compress teacher model outputs. We demonstrate that existing learning algorithms can be directly adapted to function effectively within this compressive learning framework. Furthermore, we propose an efficient student model training algorithm grounded in convex optimization principles. Empirical results across various scenarios confirm that Compressive Learning substantially lowers both the sample count and computational complexity needed for high-quality student model distillation.

This study examines a model of immigration-fueled species competition, represented mathematically by a nonlinear diffusion equation with two competing species. We provide a representation theorem for an associated measure-valued associate and establish the model's well-posedness. Additionally, we analyze the long-term dynamics of the immigration process within the competition framework.

We investigate the von Neumann algebra corresponding to the local structures within specific regions of the frustration-free ground states in the $D_2$ and $Z_2$ lattice models on a square grid. Our findings for both the D2 and Z2 systems indicate that these local structures form a Type II$_\infty$ von Neumann algebra. In contrast, for the D1 system, we establish that the local structures constitute a Type I factor.

We suggest a strategy to induce and amplify optomechanical entanglement within the cavity magnomechanical framework. This approach relies on introducing controlled phase shifts between optomechanical cavity modes through an external electromagnetic field, thereby facilitating direct mechanical-to-optical conversion of entanglement. Our proposal demonstrates the ability to generate closed-loop entanglement and effectively sustains the coherent state of the mechanical oscillator. Finally, we examine the impact of practical imperfections on optical entanglement generation, confirming the viability and resilience of this method.

This study details the construction of the first complete set of triple-collinear one-loop operations for mapping color and spin-space structures in massless next-to-next-to-next-to-leading order (NNNLO) QCD. These operations, which include splitting, joining, and swapping actions, function as local changes to the color/spin topology that fully factorize the spin-dependent parts of color-permuted or helicity-independent components. Furthermore, these operations enable a fully factorized representation of triple-collinear one-loop radiation in fully exclusive massless N$^{2}$LO QCD, a result that generalizes the known double-collinear cases applicable to next-to-next-to-leading order (N$^{2}$LO) QCD.

"An implementation for obtaining the general resolution of singularities, known as Gueneral Neron Desingularization (GND), is presented in the case of one-dimensional local rings. This procedure is demonstrated within a package named Nonsinguarization, which resides inside the broader ring theory library, Notring.

In classical Islamic civilization, the path of the Sun's daily motion was central to religious observance. Historically, Muslims have determined the holy direction (qibla) for prayer and the start of the lunar month based on the new moon sighting, with both tasks requiring precise orientation to Mecca and the calendar month, respectively. Consequently, establishing prayer times and defining the calendar have always depended on solar observations. This essay explores the relationship between astronomy and religion within the early Islamic world, highlighting how advancements in science were driven by these spiritual necessities.

This paper investigates a dual-mode (D2M) communication system where a D2D pair shares the spectrum with a macro base station (MBS) supporting multiple single-antenna users. An intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) is integrated to facilitate spectrum sharing, with design goals focused on maximizing the sum rates of the D2D pair and the MBS while ensuring each achieves at least its respective minimum rate target. The resulting optimization problem is non-convex due to the coupling between beamforming vectors and IRS phase shifts, alongside the discrete nature of the MBS operating modes. To address these challenges, we propose an iterative algorithm that alternates between optimizing beamforming and phase shifts and selecting the MBS mode. Specifically, an iterative method with a convergence proof is developed to optimize beamforming and phase shifts for a fixed MBS mode, while beamsearch is employed to determine the optimal MBS mode configuration. Simulation results confirm that the suggested framework effectively enhances the sum rates of both the D2D pair and the MBS.

Driven by the growing demand for remote, non-contact analysis of sample behaviors, we introduce "Virtual Lab on a Chip," an initiative aimed at miniaturizing the tools and apparatuses typically required in scientific research. Initially, this framework was validated through the distance-based remote characterization of fluidic mixing and thermal expansion phenomena. Subsequently, we sought to enhance the fidelity of these analyses by integrating a 2D Laser Doppler Vibrometry (LDV) system with an image-processing algorithm. This combination allows for the simultaneous measurement of both in-plane and out-of-plane sample velocities. The resulting data is processed to generate comprehensive 2D velocity and displacement field maps, which are utilized to identify and track specific sample characteristics, such as the speed of propagating mechanical waves.

We establish that for any finite collection of variables, there exists a symmetric binary relation in a finite structure such that the set of spectra for its first-order formulas using up to that many variables forms only finitely many arithmetic progressions, where each shares the same common difference. This result generalizes an earlier finding by Kiefer, and the structure presented is a subset of the integer plane equipped with a specific equivalence relation.

Although the spatial resolution of Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs) has approached the sub-Ångström threshold, achieving further improvements demands better control over the phase of electron wavefunctions. This study introduces a novel class of electrostatic components, programmable electrostatic phase plates (PEPPs), designed to manipulate the phase of incident wavefunctions with high precision. These devices utilize an array of vertical microscale needles biased with specific voltages to form phase-correcting structures. We present a quantitative analysis of the device performance, including its phase shift capabilities, aperture size, and spatial frequency response, alongside a detailed examination of how phase plate parameters influence contrast within the exit wave of a spherical aberration-corrected TEM operating at 300 kV. Our results indicate that PEPPs can successfully compensate for spherical aberration ($C_s$) with a potential spatial aperture of approximately 0.15 Å, offering significant advantages for imaging and characterizing both static and dynamic samples.

This work reviews established and emerging concepts in theories regarding physical computability and physical complexity, tracing their development from foundational research by Feynman and Landauer to more recent advancements.

This work presents an extensible algorithm for deriving closed-form formulas of exact solutions to the discrete, diffusion equation on an $d$-dimensional hypercubic lattice. The approach begins with establishing the equation in vector notation and defining a probability distribution for an $n$-step random walk, where a walker can move to any of the $2d$ adjacent sites with equal likelihood. The general formula determining the precise number of ways to reach an $n$-step walk to a specific position is $\frac{n!}{(n/2+d r)_r^3} \prod_{i=1}^{d} \left( \frac{n/2+d r-i}{n-2i+2} \right)^2$, where $r$ represents the distance from the origin. By applying multivariate Faà di Bruno's formula, this formulation is subsequently expressed as a trivariate hypergeometric function.

This study investigates scalar and polar gravitational quasinormal modes within scalar-tensor theories of gravity, incorporating both the black hole's quantum backreaction and the quantum nature of the scalar field. The analysis reveals that quantum back-Reaction significantly alters the standard black hole quasinormal frequencies. Specifically, when the quantum correction to the black hole mass is substituted into the classical frequency formulas, the resulting changes are substantial. The findings indicate that the imaginary components of these modes—representing decay rates—are markedly more negative in the post-quantum regime compared to classical predictions. Consequently, decaying occurs at a much faster rate in the post-quantum era. Additionally, the research explores the influence of the scalar field's quantum characteristics on the frequency's real part, which characterizes the oscillatory behavior. The oscillation period for both scalar and polar gravitational modes in the post-quantum regime is observed to be significantly shorter than in the classical case.

This study investigates the thermodynamics of a two-dimensional quantum system composed of massless Dirac fermions interacting with repulsive Coulomb forces through ab initio calculations grounded in the Schwinger-Dyson/Bethe-Salpeter framework. Our analysis reveals low-temperature specific heat consistent with a gapless ground state, whereas pseudogap behavior emerges under moderate coupling strengths. Additionally, we identify Coulomb-induced mass generation for both Dirac fermions and excitations near the $K$ point in momentum space, finding that Coulomb interactions predominantly suppress the intrinsic fermion mass rather than enhancing it.

This paper introduces a new dataset and a corresponding speech synthesis framework designed for article-level text-to-speech. The dataset comprises approximately 1.2 million paragraphs sourced from news articles, with an average length of 500 characters. To handle this extended duration, we developed a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) based TTS model that incorporates a novel duration control mechanism. This mechanism breaks the input into small segments, enabling the GAN to generate audio correspondingly. Additionally, we employ a Transformer-based unit to acurately predict the duration of these segments. The resulting system produces natural speech with an average generation time of 3.8 seconds per paragraph.

We introduce a resampling algorithm for projection predictive inference that enables variable selection and offer a critical examination of its theoretical underpinnings. Although widely utilized in practice, projection methods currently lack a rigorous theoretical framework. We establish the theoretical basis for projection techniques under generic Bayesian Gaussian process models and the broader context of Bayesian linear models. Our analysis reveals that while these projections generally induce only approximate sparsity, they achieve exact sparsity within Gaussian process classification tasks. We further evaluate a variety of sampling approaches and identify an innovative one, assessing their performance across classification and regression problems with diverse characteristics. Comparisons with standard selection methods demonstrate that projection inference not only identifies relevant variables more quickly but also enhances both predictive accuracy and computational efficiency.

Deep learning has emerged as a highly effective approach for numerous pattern recognition tasks, yet recent investigations have revealed inherent vulnerabilities within Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), specifically their susceptibility to adversarial examples. This paper explores the generation of such adversarial samples using two primary methods: (1) a differential attack that introduces minimal, human-imperceptible noise to the original image, and (2) a reconstruction attack that forces the network to classify an image as the target label. The primary goal is to evaluate the network's resilience against these threats. The study's outcomes are instrumental in identifying specific weaknesses within the network, thereby guiding subsequent improvements. The proposed methodology is validated on the MNIST dataset using a convolutional neural network, with further testing and analysis conducted on the CIFAR-10 dataset employing an established CNN architecture.

This study examines the propagation of conspiracy theories within Twitter networks, utilizing a dataset of 1,000 conspiracy-specific tweets and their associated networks. By analyzing the structural properties of these networks and the user profiles involved, the research investigates the relationship between a user's climate change beliefs and their propensity to engage with conspiracy content. Results indicate that conspiracy-related networks are generally sparse, small in size, and highly centralized, with the majority of such networks centered around individual conspiracy theories. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that the distribution of conspiracy belief propagation is highly skewed, with users holding lower levels of climate change belief demonstrating greater sharing activity compared to those with stronger belief levels.

This study investigates dark matter production within the proton-proton collisions of the LHC, utilizing a simplified framework where dark matter interacts with Standard Model quarks through light scalar or pseudoscalar mediators. By analyzing the kinematic distributions of the produced dark matter particles, we derive robust lower limits on the mediator mass ranging from 10 to 100 GeV/c² for a fixed coupling constant. These results demonstrate that employing distributions for missing transverse momentum and transverse momentum offers superior exclusion power compared to the standard practice of relying solely on the transverse mass distribution.

In an arbitrary Krull-Schmidt exangulated category, we establish that the Auslander-Reiten n-exangle corresponding to an Auslander-Reiten triangle (for any $n \ge 3$) is unique. Furthermore, we demonstrate dualities: dualizing the $n$-exangle direction yields an Auslander-Reiten $(n+2)$-exangle, which remains unique. These findings generalize the classical results of Ringel and Xiao regarding triangulated categories and are applicable beyond triangles to broader exangulated settings.

In numerous economic settings, instruments for multiple unordered treatment levels are utilized to identify and estimate the causal impacts of those treatments. This paper presents a nonparametric framework for such multiple, coarsened endogenous, and unordered treatment instruments, allowing for arbitrary unobserved heterogeneity regarding treatment responses. The proposed setup uses post-stratification to create local identification regions surrounding the true parameters of interest, such as the LATE distribution and average treatment effects. Furthermore, we derive the sharpest possible bounds for these targets given fixed instruments, demonstrating that our bounds are tight within this specific class of models. Finally, we develop multiple new parametric families—structured to satisfy the necessary and sufficient conditions for our local bounds—to facilitate numerical illustration of the method.

Creating antiprotons with angular momentum is essential for engaging in scattering experiments with antimatter. However, the production methods currently available generate particles in a statistical mixture of different spin states, rendering angular momentum identification mandatory. This note introduces a technique to identify these spin states using the angular distribution of annihilation events involving antiprotons.

We examine the hypothesis that the formation of close binary systems within multiple star systems results from differential accretion during the early stages of evolution. In this scenario, the common envelope phase of the third body in a hierarchical triple acts as the separation point, with angular momentum transfer causing the inner pair to shrink while the outer pair expands. We analyze the outcomes of N-body simulations involving 1000 randomly generated triples, each containing an inner binary and a distant tertiary, to determine the frequency of this outcome. Our findings indicate that the likelihood of differential accretion is highly dependent on the mass ratio between the inner binary and the outer companion. Specifically, when the inner binary is less massive, the process is more probable, suggesting that close binaries form more often in systems hosted by low-mass binaries. Furthermore, tertiary ejection is more common in cases where the inner binary possesses lower mass. Finally, we observe that the final orbital parameters of the resulting binaries are not uniform; rather, they cluster around specific values for semi-major axes and eccentricities.

"We investigate intrinsically flat spacetimes that exhibit symmetry under isometry groups with dimensions ranging from 2 to 4. These intrinsically flat models serve as valuable baseline references against which intrinsically curved spacetimes can be compared. We apply this analysis to intrinsically flat solutions of the Einstein-Maxwell equations to derive the intrinsically flat section of the well-known Bertotti-Robinson metric. Furthermore, we discuss the significance of these intrinsically flat geometries within the context of cosmology."

Image restoration and image segmentation are two fundamental computer vision tasks that have seen significant advancements in recent years. By combining them, one can address more complex real-world challenges, such as restoring degraded images of missing structures or segments within missing areas. This paper presents a unified framework that integrates image restoration and segmentation models. We specifically investigate a new cross-task segmentation and restoration task: restoring missing structures in low-dose CT scans. By jointly optimizing segmentation and restoration through mutual benefits, our approach yields superior performance compared to standalone methods. We release the first public low-dose CT dataset, which includes ground truth for both tasks. Experiments confirm that our joint model significantly outperforms existing separate segmentation and restoration techniques.

We investigate the determination of black hole mass and spin in Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) through their electromagnetic spectra. By analyzing the AGN's time-domain light curves, one can infer the black hole's spin and mass. We begin by outlining the theoretical underpinnings of this approach and its reliance on the relativistic blazar model. We then present a method to extract these parameters from light curves using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm, which fits the model parameters by minimizing the residuals between observed and simulated data. We further demonstrate that, for blazars exhibiting quasi-periodic variability, this technique offers a robust means of constraining the black hole's spin and mass.

Neuromorphic systems have garnered significant attention for their potential to emulate the energy-efficient, fault-tolerant, and adaptable characteristics of the human brain. To date, research has primarily focused on developing novel hardware architectures alongside corresponding software frameworks. This paper introduces an open-source, scalable, and extensible neuromorphic System-on-Chip (SoC) designed to facilitate integrated hardware and software co-optimization for neuromorphic applications. Our proposed architecture employs a many-core paradigm featuring specialized, reconfigurable microcontrollers that mimic neural components, coupled with a unified, scalable communication substrate. To date, our fully integrated, hardware/software-coupled architecture has been realized and validated through a comprehensive simulation environment built upon an established software stack. Leveraging our publicly available and evolving Python-based software framework, our hardware-in-the-loop (HITL) architecture enables rapid prototyping and testing of both individual components and the system as a whole. This capability is expected to empower researchers to accelerate the development of new algorithms and hardware designs within the realm of neuromorphic engineering.

A prominent noise storm originating from solar type-I bursts was detected by the Radio and Telescope of Solar and Heliospheric Investigation (RHESSI) on 2014-09-11. This event coincided with a microflare and a compact brightening observed in the X-ray band, pinpointing the noise source to the flare site. The source exhibited two distinct evolutionary phases: a gradual phase and a sudden phase. During the gradual phase, the source parameters displayed a sawtooth-like pattern, which was analyzed using a linear feedback model. This model revealed that the source's evolution resulted from competition between a positive and a negative feedback loop. Furthermore, the transition from the gradual to the sudden phase was driven by the dominance of the positive feedback loop.

A magneto-optical trap (MOT) serves as a fundamental instrument in atomic physics, enabling the confinement of vast numbers of free atoms and their subsequent cooling to micro-Kelvin temperatures. This work details a new, fully 3D numerical simulation of a MOT, developed to investigate the complex, non-linear interactions between laser light and atomic matter. Utilizing a fully coupled Maxwell-Bloch formulation, the study examines these atomic-light dynamics across diverse configurations of atomic number density and optical intensity. The results indicate that under conditions of high density and intensity, significant deviations arise between ray-tracing approaches and a rigorous propagation method, leading to the formation of distinct photorefractive structures within the simulation.

This study investigates the accretion of a spherically symmetric gas cloud with uniform density and uniform random or ordered velocity fields by a growing black hole. The cloud's mass accretion rate is compared against the predictions of the Bondi model. The analysis reveals that angular momentum in the cloud can significantly lower the Bondi accretion rate by orders of magnitude, even when the total angular momentum of the system is conserved. The findings demonstrate that black hole masses can vary widely in this context, with accretion occurring at rates far below the Bondi prediction as a function of the cloud's properties. The paper provides analytical expressions for the minimum black hole mass in these scenarios and offers a physical explanation for how internal cloud flows and angular momentum influence the accretion dynamics.

We examine the radiative decay of a neutral excited atom approaching a ground-based conducting plane, addressing both electric and magnetic dipole moments. By applying the worldline formalism coupled with the pseudo-quantum action path-integral method, we determine the rate of spontaneous emission. This process involves calculating the spontaneous emission of an isolated atom first, followed by evaluating corrections arising from a nearby plane through the perturbation expansion of the worldline electromagnetic field. Our perturbation analysis reveals that an initial order expansion in the dipole moments yields no contribution to spontaneous emission changes. Consequently, calculations must proceed to the second order in the dipole moments to capture the effects modifying the emission rate. At this second-order level, we find that the spontaneous emission rate increases when the atom is near the plane, with the magnitude of enhancement depending on the orientation of the atom's dipole moment relative to its trajectory and the distance from the surface.

We report the discovery of NGC 6231V, a massive O9.5V star located approximately 1000 AU from the center of the young cluster NGC 6231. This star is embedded within a dense, dusty molecular core that houses a compact stellar group of approximately 100 objects, including several other massive stars. Our analysis of the core's kinematics indicates that the system is still undergoing expansion. Furthermore, the O9.5V star NGC 6231V is the most luminous object in this core and is likely responsible for shaping the surrounding molecular cloud through its strong stellar winds and radiation pressure. The findings suggest that massive stars can form outside of dense clusters, a scenario that may occur in collapsing molecular cores or through dynamical interactions within young, expanding clusters.

Handwritten document images frequently suffer from degradation caused by factors such as poor pen pressure, shaky hands, substandard paper quality, and aging. These issues often compromise a document's legibility, necessitating restoration efforts to enhance readability. Although numerous deep learning approaches have been developed for this purpose, they typically rely on synthetic training data generated through convolution filtering or blending techniques. Consequently, this study introduces a new H2R-CycleGAN model for cursive image restoration that utilizes authentic degraded handwritten scans as training inputs. By employing CyclicGAN for unsupervised image-to-image translation paired with a multi-scale feature alignment loss, the method enables the translation of degraded images into handwritten text without requiring paired data. The resulting restored images are then cyclically translated back to verify their fidelity to the original input. The paper presents an end-to-end deep learning framework designed to read text from Indonesian Identity Cards (KTP) using Optical Character Recognition (OCR). The system begins by localizing the card through image segmentation, followed by applying state-of-the-art CRNN with attention mechanisms for optical character recognition. Finally, a post-processing stage utilizes dynamic dictionary matching and Tesseract engine to refine the raw OCR output. The proposed method, named Dynamic OCR (D-OCR), was evaluated on the Indonesian KTP OCR dataset, achieving an accuracy of 94.88% and an F1-score of 94.11%.

This paper introduces a novel channel tracking method for vehicular systems that utilizes sparse representation and sparse Bayesian learning (SBL). Capitalizing on the sparsity of channel characteristics, the proposed SB L framework reduces computational complexity while pilot allocation strategies are designed to enhance channel estimation performance. Furthermore, tracking accuracy is improved by the iterative refinement of channel state information derived from pilot symbols. Simulation results demonstrate that the new method outperforms existing approaches, exhibiting greater resilience to rapid channel variations and significantly higher estimation accuracy.

This paper introduces CoNet, a network designed for automatic colorization that employs only spatial image information. Since access to no adjacent pixels (making it the only neighboring context unavailable), single images, or previous frames is granted, this architecture is notably simpler than many existing solutions that depend on video sequences or complex reconstruction models. To handle the inherent ambiguity of color mapping, our method integrates multiple prior colors through the application of Markov Random Fields. Experiments conducted on the standard IGA2016 dataset indicate that CoNet surpasses other current RGB-only approaches in color space transformations.

This work introduces a numerical method for determining Artificial Neural Network (ANN) weights based on the empirical central limit theorem. We demonstrate that an established iterative algorithm can be proven correct using the evidence provided by this theorem. Additionally, our findings reveal a direct link between the training phase of backpropagation and the solution of partial differential equations. This numerical approach offers several distinct advantages: it is straightforward to implement, computationally efficient, and guarantees globally convergent results.

The ECFA panel dedicated to Early Career Researchers (ECR) was established in 2018 to champion the interests and support the professional development of junior physicists within the community. Operating under the working title "Europee," this group functions as both an information hub and a networking platform, offering insights into ECAs opportunities and fostering connections among young researchers. In this document, the European group outlines its strategic vision, proposed roadmap, and specific activities undertaken to date.

Line waves are introduced at the interface of dual electromagnetic metasurfaces, which are arranged in pairs with dual electric and magnetic characteristics and are separated by a thin dielectric layer. These line waves are non-propagating, supporting arbitrary amplitude and phase distributions, and can exist in practical applications. Introducing dual electromagnetic metasurface pairs allows for line waves with arbitrary amplitude and phase distributions, enabling line waves to form.

Learning from demonstration (LfD) has emerged as a promising framework for acquiring new skills in robotics, yet current cognitive approaches often fail to address the inherent uncertainty associated with human actions and intent. To overcome this limitation, this study introduces a multi-agent cognitive system capable of robustly acquiring human skills despite ambiguous and noisy observational data. Our proposed solution employs a attention mechanism-driven multiple hypothesis tracker to manage noisy inputs and constructs a multi-agent reinforcement learning architecture where a dedicated learner agent acquires the skill while corresponding interpreter agents analyze the human movements across multiple points-of-view simultaneously. By integrating observations from various perspectives through these concurrent interpreters, the system effectively mitigates the limitations of single-view dependencies, enabling robust skill learning under conditions of observation noise and ambiguity. Validated through experiments involving complex, real-world demonstrations recorded by a humanoid robot, the results confirm the superior performance and robustness of our multi-agent cognitive approach compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

A bias-reduced estimator for the population-level mean is developed to minimize the asymptotic bias in a bias-reduced population mean estimate when applied to large-scale linear models. This development is extended to include bias-reduced frameworks for median regression and biased-homogeneous regression. The asymptotic properties of these bias-reduced estimators are established, demonstrating that they possess strong statistical validity. The proposed bias-reduced estimator is implemented through a bias-reduced least squares method, which is applicable to various types of linear models. Relation extraction (RE) involves identifying relational knowledge between entities within text, a task that is typically addressed by first converting sentences into feature-rich symbolic representations before predicting the specific relation type. Although these hand-crafted features have historically driven RE systems, they often fail to fully capture the nuanced language required for relation extraction. In contrast, this study introduces an end-to-end neural RE framework that leverages embeddings for word pieces to automatically generate necessary features for the prediction process. By training a relation classifier over views containing varying numbers of features, the model learns to identify the most informative features for the given data. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach outperforms prior state-of-the-art RE systems.

We investigate the ground-state dissociation temperature of quarkonia within an anisotropic N-dimensional background, extending the analysis to higher orders. Using the N-dimensional Schrödinger equation, we determine the binding energy of quarkonium ground states, applying both the potential model and the AdS/QCD framework. Our results demonstrate that quarkonium dissociation is sensitive to both N-dimensional effects and background anisotropy. Specifically, we find that increasing the total dimensionality lowers the dissociation temperature, while anisotropy further reduces this temperature relative to the isotropic case, reducing it progressively as anisotropy grows. Additionally, the binding energy gap between J/\psi and \chi_{bJ} states is notably larger in higher dimensions compared to four-dimensional space.

This study examines the magnetic and electric dipole moments of Tb$_3$RuO$_7$ using neutron diffraction. The compound exhibits a complex structure with multiple magnetic sublattices, characterized by ordered moments of 7.5 $\mu_B$ for Tb, 1.2 $\mu_B$ for Ru$_1$, and 2.2 $\mu_B$ for Ru$_2$. The observed ordering follows a commensurate hexagonal pattern with space group P6$_3$/mmc. The magnetic moments of the terbium ions display a strong temperature dependence, whereas the ruthenium moments remain largely constant down to 1.5 K before showing a slight increase at lower temperatures. Additionally, the research investigates the coexistence of magnetic and electric dipole moments in this material, offering insights into potential applications in electric and magnetic control of multiferroic systems.

This study introduces a novel machine learning-based approach to analyzing and modeling the internal signal representations of visual and auditory content, specifically focusing on videos and image sequences. We explore a dual multi-layer perceptron (MLP) framework where a primary MLP encapsulates a latent latent space shared sequentially with a secondary MLP tailored to specific video frames. The structure leverages latent space trajectories to reconstruct entire video sequences. We examine various supervised and unsupervised training strategies for these models, evaluating their efficacy in restoring corrupted or missing video data. The work also investigates applying this representation system to enhance compression efficiency and facilitates downstream tasks such as video analysis.

While existing covariate shift adaptation techniques predominantly rely on labeled source domain data, this paper introduces a novel approach by integrating adaptation with semi-supervised learning to harness unlabeled target data. This combination not only reduces dependency on large volumes of target labeled data but also enhances source-unseen regions through domain alignment. We achieve this integration via a mutual adaptation framework that incorporates semi-supervised learning, enabling bidirectional adaptation alongside the correction of source domain corrections based on domain embedding distances. Experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets confirm that our method outperforms state-of-the-art adaptation techniques.

Recent research has increasingly examined the geometric properties linking deep learning model performance to their weights in weight space. This work extends that investigation by defining the broader "deep learning systems framework," which encompasses not only the model and training data but also the algorithm, architecture, and other relevant factors. We analyze the corresponding system geometry, demonstrating that the deep learning setup can be represented through various mathematical geometries, including metric, ordered, and topological structures. Specifically, we apply Rao-Blackwellize metrics to define a distance measure within the system, thereby enabling the construction of a topological layout that maps a model's performance across different input configurations. Our findings indicate a strong correlation between this learned system topology and existing topological definitions, such as those found in support vector machines. Ultimately, this approach offers a comprehensive view of deep learning systems, bridging the gap between prior geometric studies of individual models and the broader contextual factors influencing their behavior.

Let $d$ represent the discriminant of a number field $K$. This paper investigates ambiguous principal ideals within $K$ that remain primitive when extended to the ring of integers of the Hilbert 2-class field of $K$. We analyze how the presence of generators for these specific ideal classes is influenced by the $p$-rank of the 2-part of $K$'idele class group (where $p$ is an odd prime) and whether $K$ contains the square roots of $-1$ or $\pm 2$. Additionally, we apply these findings to refine our understanding of the $p$-rank (for an odd prime $p$) of the 2-part of $K$'idele class group.

Recent research has explored integrating external information into deep neural network (DNN) architectures to enhance their performance. This study investigates such techniques within the context of jet substructure tagging at hadron colliders, specifically aiming to improve jet-kinematics-independent classifiers. We demonstrate that incorporating expert-derived variables through an established retraining pipeline yields significant improvements in classifier performance. Furthermore, we present a classifier that successfully merges DNN outputs with a traditional multivariate analysis (MVA) technique, successfully combining the strengths of both machine learning paradigms.

For any positive integer r, the r-associated Stirling number of the second kind quantifies the count of partitions of the set {1, ..., n} where no block size falls between 1 and r. These numbers satisfy r differential difference equations, known as Numiara's equatio ns, which have been utilized to define and investigate r polynomial associated Stirling numbers. In this work, we introduce r differential associated Stirling numbers through a partition function that incorporates n, r, and x, where x represents a real variable. These numbers obey a set of r associated Miki differences equations, which in turn yield r associated B ell polynomials that obey a set of r associated Miki differences equations, which in turn generate r associated B ell polynomials. Finally, we explore the properties of and relationships among these r associated B ell polynomials.

This study introduces a novel methodology for the symbolic calculation of layer group attributes, specifically targeting classification, symmetry operations, and layers. The layer group, an extension of the crystallographic space group, functions as a two-dimensional group by allowing a 3rd dimension of invariance.
