We introduce a family of first-order differential operators that function as "momentum," defined on intrinsically curved manifolds. Specifically, we establish that the manifold's geometric structure is determined by a specific connection, the torsion of which corresponds precisely to the manifold's curvature. Furthermore, we prove that the commutation relations between these intrinsically linked momentum operators are governed by the underlying curvature. Under the condition that the manifold is of compact type, additional relations arise involving the topology of the manifold, specifically utilizing a closed 2-form representing an integer class.

This study examines the spectral function of the half-filled attractive Hubbard model on a square lattice, utilizing a Monte Carlo method that leverages the dual representation to generate sign-free configurations. We analyze the sign problem's intensity across various auxiliary loop lengths, observing its disappearance due to lack of negativity when the loop length is even. By averaging short-loop configurations to infer a coarse-grained picture and employing a selected configuration approach to recover specific longer loops, we investigate spectral properties. Our findings reveal that short loops fail to capture long-range correlations adequately, yet the selected Monte Carlo algorithm produces a spectral function consistent with world-sheet scaling predictions.

We introduce a novel framework for the composite Higgs model that relies on a scalar field. This field functions as a composite of fermions, emerging as a non-perturbative solution to the sigma model in two dimensions. Dimensional deconstruction serves as the mechanism for elevating this two-dimensional solution into four dimensions. Within this framework, the profile of the scalar field in two dimensions dictates the mass spectrum of composite fermions.

Virtual-Reality systems frequently encounter user fatigue stemming from an imbalance between extensive virtual movements and restricted physical motion. To address this, we introduce Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations (VPPMs), a novel approach to enhance the virtual-to-physical mapping in head-mounted displays by leveraging perceptual illusions. These manipulations allow for the decoupling of virtual and physical movement scales, thereby accommodating a broader range of virtual motion within limited bodily constraints. We evaluated the effectiveness and usability of VPPM through two studies involving 36 participants performing continuous walking and climbing simulations. Findings indicate that applying scaled movement transformations significantly reduces perceived physical exertion without compromising immersion or increasing motion sickness. Additionally, user preferences for specific scaling factors vary based on task demands, demonstrating the flexibility of this technique.

We investigate methods for adding new languages to existing multilingual models. Our results demonstrate that pre-training continues effectively even with very limited data, and our experiments with zero-shot German confirm its viability. We find that token embeddings transfer better than layer weights across languages, and that re-initializing transformer layers outperforms simply copying them. Additionally, we show that adapter modules are more effective than full model fine-tuning for domain adaptation in newly added languages. These insights are validated through the inclusion of German and Russian into our model, which expands GPT-3's coverage to 27 languages total.

Recent research indicates that the total mass of a parent core is a critical factor in the formation of binary stellar systems. This study utilizes the piecewise power-law model to analyze the mass distribution of binary fragments, with specific attention to how the mass of the parent core influences fragment mass. Our findings demonstrate that binary fragments are most likely to form from parent cores with masses between 10 and 20 solar masses ($M_{\odot}$). Furthermore, binary fragments originating from parent cores exceeding 20 $M_{\odot}$ tend to have higher masses than those from lower-mass cores. We also observe that binary systems with primary components under 5 $M_{\odot}$ are predominantly formed from parent cores below 10 $M_{\odot}$. These results offer valuable insights for understanding the mechanisms of binary stellar formation.

This research introduces a modified version of the m-Arbitrary-Neural Network Independent Component Analysis (m-ar-K-FastICA) algorithm, designed to enhance its performance in extracting features from random environments. This method integrates the capabilities of both the original m-ar-K-FastICA and Arbitrary-Neural Network ICA (ANN-ICA) approaches. By leveraging the nonlinear mapping and independent component separation strengths of ANN-ICA alongside the improved convergence speed of m-AFICA, the proposal optimizes computational efficiency. The outcomes demonstrate that this algorithm excels in feature extraction under stochastic conditions, delivering superior results in terms of processing time and accuracy compared to conventional ICA techniques.

This research demonstrates that if Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPT) can distinguish between non-isomorphic pairs of polynomial-sized graphs selected from a finite class $\mathcal{C}$, then the bounded-degree extended polynomial calculus (EPC) admits a sound refutation method of bounded degree for unsatisfiable systems of conjunctions of quantifier-free first-order sentences belonging to $\mathcal{C}$. When applied to the non-isomorphic pair of twin-free graphs previously introduced by Nonnenmacher and Schaefer, this result establishes sound refutations in the bounded-degree extended polynomial calculus that are strictly of limited degree for their unsatisfiable theories.

An association of a ring is defined as a multiplicative subgroup within its units. The covering number, denoted as $\sigma(R)$ for a ring $R$ equipped with identity, represents the minimum cardinality of an associated set $C$ such that the product of the difference between any element in the ring and an element in $C$ yields zero ($(\mathbb{R}-c)c=0$ for all $c \in \mathbb{R}$). This concept was initially investigated by Erd\H{o}s and Selfridge within the context of the integers $\mathbb{Z}$, subsequently extended to various fields including associative algebras, commutative rings, and non-commutative structures. In this study, we examine the covering numbers specific to split-real quaternion algebras and certain classes of matrix rings defined over the integers modulo $n$ ($\mathbb{Z}_n$).

Social media generates an overwhelming volume of user-generated content daily, creating a challenge for fact-checkers to identify and address misinformation promptly. This paper presents a new approach to efficiently fact-check emerging rumors by integrating content analysis with cross-platform propagation data. Our proposed propagation-driven method targets the detection of false claims by analyzing the propagation patterns of associated content across different platforms.

Identifying significant occurrences in real-time social media data streams is crucial for a broad spectrum of applications, including disaster response, security surveillance, and event detection. To address this, we introduce a novel method that leverages statistical significance to identify such incidents. Our approach employs a statistical framework to pinpoint sudden shifts in the co-appearance frequencies of entities, with the ability to detect notable events ranging from natural disasters and sporting events to celebrity deaths and terrorist attacks. By utilizing efficient, in-stream processing, we can rapidly discover these events as they unfold. Furthermore, we have developed a specialized statistical test to mitigate the impact of noisy, irrelevant entity mentions. Extensive experiments conducted on both real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches.

We introduce a novel, robust, and analytical technique for cosmological parameter estimation that leverages the skew-spectrum, a real-valued function dependent on the bispectrum along with the line-of-sight wavenumber $k_\parallel$. By weighting the skew-spectrum with a specific window function, we construct a bispectrum-inspired power spectrum capable of capturing distinctive, non-linear statistical signatures. This approach offers new access to cosmic structure information, notably enhancing sensitivity to neutrino species and their masses. Furthermore, the weighted skew-spectrum facilitates efficient computation of the bispectrum's impact on the matter power spectrum through the standard, one-dimensional configuration.

This study introduces a new framework for adversarial training within Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). Traditional approaches to generating robust BNN posteriors often rely on deterministic techniques, such as the deterministic reparameterization trick, which undermines the inherent uncertainty of BNNs. Our proposed method, named adversarial dynamic vector scaling (A-DVS), offers a solution by refining both the mean and variance of the posteriors over neural network weights. This is achieved through gradient-based optimization of a adversarial loss function that incorporates both expected performance and performance variance under adversarial conditions. Empirical results indicate that images perturbed with the Fast Gradient Sign (FGSM) attack demonstrate superior robustness using models trained with A-DVS.

The COVID-19 pandemic and the subsequent misinformation it spawned have severely disrupted public health. Online rumors, particularly those spread via social media, can cause significant social disruption, with the Chinese social platform Sina Weibo becoming a primary vector for such falsehoods. This study investigates the mechanisms driving the propagation of false information on Weibo, focusing specifically on rumors that emerged during the Wuhan lockdown in early 2020. By analyzing a dataset of 1,000 rumor posts, the research identifies the critical roles played by information relevance, timing, and the initial number of comments in fostering viral spread. Furthermore, the examination of comment thread structures reveals that comment relevance and the presence of authoritative accounts are pivotal factors in determining whether rumors gain widespread traction.

This paper introduces a novel approach to classifying hyperspectral pixels through nearest neighbor analysis in the feature space, utilizing low-rank approximation techniques. The study evaluates the performance of three dimensionality reduction methods—Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), and Partial Least Squares (PLS)—on the Indian Museum dataset, which contains 250 visible-light cubes from 105 distinct material types. Results indicate that a PCA-reduced subspace of approximately 5% of the original size achieves over 90% accuracy, with the PLS-optimized subspace surpassing this benchmark by reaching nearly 95% accuracy. The research also examines how compression ratios and the specific dimensionality reduction technique influence outcomes, revealing that PLS consistently outperforms both PCA and LDA across various experimental conditions.

The recent "winner takes all" pruning approach identifies a minimal subnetwork within over-parameterized models that retains full accuracy and performance, a finding that has spurred interest in the broader task of enhancing network efficiency through structural adaptations. This work presents a novel framework for the "structural evolution" of neural networks, capable of transforming any initial architecture into an optimized form tailored to the specific validation data. Central to this methodology is a new concept known as the "structural fitness landscape," a space of potential topographies where the most promising individual structures are isolated. By accessing this landscape, the proposed system can refine existing architectures into higher-performing variants.

The chemical shift of a protein's amide proton is a critical indicator of its structural state, as it is highly sensitive to the local hydrogen bonding environment. While this parameter is routinely employed to validate predicted protein conformations, there is currently no established method for calculating these values from ab initio protein models. Addressing this gap, we introduce a novel technique that derives amide proton chemical shifts by analyzing models generated through ab initio assembly. This approach utilizes a chemical change matrix to determine the contributions of individual residues' environments to the overall chemical shift. We demonstrate that the resulting values closely align with experimental data, achieving a correlation coefficient of r = 0.92. Furthermore, the chemical shifts generated by our method effectively identify the most accurate structures within sets of ab initio predictions.

The loss function is integral to the backpropagation process and determines how a deep neural network's parameters are updated during supervised classification training. Although various options exist, the standard cross-entropy loss remains prevalent in practice. This study investigates the impact of alternative losses on classification performance through both empirical evaluation and theoretical analysis. We theoretically demonstrate that the commonly used mean squared error (MSE) loss can result in suboptimal classification outcomes within a deep neural network context. Furthermore, through extensive experiments on multiple datasets with various network architectures, we confirm these empirical observations. Our results indicate that network performance utilizing MSE is often surpassed significantly by other loss functions, thereby underscoring the critical importance of carefully selecting an appropriate loss function for a given task.

Investigating correlated electron systems demands accurate handling of multi-leg correlations, which parquet theory addresses by unifying various resummation techniques. We introduce a new hierarchical four-point parquet scheme that consistently implements a fully symmetric, fully quartic-runtge resummation of two-leg, four-point, and six-point correlations. Furthermore, this approach ensures strict adherence to particle number conservation and the associated continuity equations.

A semimetal-to-excitonic-insulator transition is signaled by the emergence of a complex order parameter featuring a nontrivial topological structure, which generates a gap in the excitation spectrum. This study introduces a model for such a phase within a two-dimensional lattice composed of coupled, charge-neutral bilayers of metals. By employing a variational approach to determine the ground-state energy, we demonstrate that the system self-organizes into an excitonic insulator characterized by a helical order parameter with a nontrivial hedgehog topology, resulting in a gapped spectrum. Furthermore, we show that the system's energy is minimized when the helical winding number reaches a nontrivial $2\pi$ value, corresponding to a full $2\pi$ spiral. This mechanism for minimizing energy via a $2\pi$ helical order parameter is a distinctive feature of chargeless双层 lattices, as opposed to single layers where the minimum occurs at winding numbers that are fractional multiples of $2\pi$.

To enhance community safety, various organizations have launched reporting platforms allowing citizens to notify authorities about local hazards. Although these tools offer significant safety benefits, they often suffer from sparse user engagement, resulting in suboptimal response rates. Our research investigates the impact of automated, personalized emotional support provided by system dispatchers on improving these response rates. Specifically, we introduce EmOS—a novel system designed to deliver tailored emotional assistance to users submitting reports. Comprehensive experiments conducted on a real-world dataset demonstrate that integrating EmOS boosts the response rate by 10.7%, a statistically significant increase.

This study examines the doped topological insulator Bi$_2$Se$_3$ using high-resolution tunneling spectroscopy, revealing a band structure characterized by band inversion and strong spin-orbit coupling. Analysis of temperature-dependent spectra identifies a superconducting gap exhibiting an isotropic s-wave symmetry. These findings suggest Bi$_2$Se$_3$ represents a new class of materials, characterized by topological band structures, high spin-orbit coupling, and fully gapped s-wave superconductivity.

Active learning (AL) is a semi-supervised framework designed to build an optimal classifier using the fewest possible labeled data points. Contemporary AL methods typically employ one of two approaches to choose which instances to acquire: they either target regions of high uncertainty in the current model or focus on samples most similar to already labeled data. This study introduces a novel query strategy that combines these two methods, aiming to select both highly informative and representative data points. Specifically, we propose a prototype-based prototype embedding network to identify prototypes within support sets, thereby reducing variance. By simultaneously measuring similarity to these prototypes to gauge uncertainty and leveraging the confidence of the model itself, we create a balanced selection mechanism. Empirical results across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This study introduces a novel metric known as loudness complexity to quantify the dynamic shifts in musical intensity. By analyzing the standard deviation of loudness within both songs and musical bars, the research examines historical trends from the 1960s to the 2000s. The findings reveal a marked decrease in average loudness complexity over these decades, a development the authors associate with the increasing standardization of music production. The paper further compares these historical patterns against current chart-topping songs and contrasts them with trends in other cultural domains to offer a comprehensive perspective on musical evolution.

We examine a stochastic process involving the formation of blocks, beginning with the first element in an isolated block. Subsequent integers either extend the current block by joining it or initiate entirely new blocks. The likelihood that the next integer joins the $i$-th block (of size $i$) is governed by the function $f(i)$, with the complementary probability assigned to starting a new block. This framework encompasses numerous well-known combinatorial structures, including partitions defined by restricted growth functions, set partitions, permutations, and various families of trees. The analysis yields general asymptotic results regarding the distribution of block counts, which apply to these diverse models. Specifically, we derive limit theorems for scenarios where the relative change in $f(i)$ remains bounded, alongside a corresponding compound Poisson approximation. Furthermore, we explore the regime where $f(i)$ grows rapidly enough to yield a normal approximation for the number of blocks.

"Semantic countermodels are employed to validate the completeness of systematic proof procedures in intuitionistic logic. We introduce a streamlined, semantic-based counterexample for the completeness of systematic proof search regarding Peano Arithmetic's intuitionistic natural deduction, thereby demonstrating that even within this highly regulated framework, non-theorems can erroneously appear provable. Furthermore, we utilize counterexample analysis to introduce—on a minimal scale—the semantic principle of inverse inference in intuitionistic natural deduction and examine its relationship with completeness when applied strictly.

Human preference is central to AI, yet traditional collection methods relying on direct comparisons or explicit numerical ratings are burdensome, often causing non-experts to quit or provide unreliable data. To address this, we introduce an innovative, comparison-based preference gathering technique that leverages the "2-choices-2-images" paradigm. By prompting users to select their favored option from pairs of images twice, the method effectively filters out noise inherent in single comparisons. This approach not only significantly reduces user cognitive load but also enhances data quality by naturally eliciting consistent ordinal rankings. Our framework utilizes these preferences to train a reward model through direct optimization and a critic via implicit feedback. Experiments demonstrate that our algorithm rivals or exceeds current state-of-the-art methods in generating image prompts, with its streamlined design proving particularly suitable for gathering reliable preferences from non-specialists.

This paper establishes a positive correlation between the core-compactness of Smyth powerspaces and the local compactness of specific topological spaces. Additionally, we introduce an equivalent characterization of locally compact spaces derived from the continuous monads associated with the Smyth powerspace construction.

This study introduces a novel class of singularities within ideal 2D fluid dynamics: vortex loops with vortex filaments that terminate at specific points. These loops arise as large-scale limit structures within the rescaled vorticity of highly rotated, rotationally symmetric, compactly supported initial velocity fields in 3D ideal fluids. The theoretical framework relies on the application of the Lagrangian Coherent Structure (LCS) method.

The AIPW estimator stands out as a powerful, double-robust, and bias-protected method for causal inference, yet its computational demands have historically limited its application to simple scenarios. Recently, Nguyen et al. (2015) introduced the nAIPW estimator, extending AIPW to handle nested counterfactuals through the use of importance weights. This research demonstrates that both the original and extended AIPW variants share eight fundamental characteristics, specifically: double robustness, bias protection, consistent misspeceration behavior, ability to reduce variance, satisfaction of linear program conditions, convergence to linear programs, and representation as influence function score processes. These findings are crucial for achieving valid statistical inference. Furthermore, we introduce a novel, non-asymptotic lower bound for estimation error that applies universally to both estimators. Based on this bound, we develop a new approach for constructing confidence intervals for nested counterfactual outcomes, offering superior performance in finite samples compared to traditional influence function-based methods.

The particle physics sector has recently experienced significant interest due to indications of possible New Physics arising from lepton flavor (LFU) violation, particularly given the clean experimental signatures associated with hadron decays involving $\tau$ leptons. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of hadronic $\tau$ decays, utilizing the most recent Particle Data Group information and incorporating additional theoretical inputs. The work provides detailed branching fraction predictions for numerous hadronic $\tau$ decays, specifically addressing non-resonant channels governed by hadronic weak currents and comparing them against recent LHCb measurements. The findings demonstrate that theoretical uncertainties are sufficiently low to enable rigorous tests of the Standard Model and to probe potential New Physics mechanisms. Furthermore, we perform a detailed examination of spin structures within hadronic $\tau$ decays to enhance sensitivity to both Standard Model dynamics and possible deviations.

This study examines the origins of low-pressure systems in a two-dimensional, periodic, and barotropically stable atmospheric circulation model governed by the Navier-Stokes equations. The analysis utilizes a stochastic parameterization approach, incorporating multiplicative white noise into the low-resolution dynamics to explore the conditions necessary for cyclogenesis. The research identifies a specific set of parameters that yield a bimodal probability distribution for low-pressure system intensity, reflecting coexisting states of stability and cyclogenesis. Furthermore, by applying a quasi-equilibrium framework, the authors derive a formula for the probability of low-intensity pressure systems transforming into deep depressions. The outcomes demonstrate that incorporating noise into the system's dynamics is essential for generating this bimodal distribution and the associated transition probability.

This study introduces a novel approach to modelling extreme values by utilizing invariance of the return level for a fixed exceedance threshold. The method constructs a new class of threshold-invariant extreme value parameters, which are employed to develop a parameter estimation technique. The resulting threshold-invariant model offers several benefits: it simplifies interpretation, minimizes the risk of mis-specifying the model, and accurately captures the dependence between extreme events.

This paper investigates offline reinforcement learning in the presence of online tampering adversaries. The adversary is constrained by a limited budget to modify a specific proportion of state-action tuples within the static dataset. Our primary goal is to identify an approximate policy that maximizes the expected reward. We demonstrate that even when the adversary compromises up to a fraction $1-\epsilon$ of the dataset, it is possible to achieve an $\epsilon$-optimal policy with probability $1-\delta$. To reach this objective, the adversary must expend at least $\Omega(\epsilon^2\delta)$ modifications. Building on this theoretical framework, the proposed algorithm is straightforward yet delivers strong performance, achieving a sample complexity of $\tilde{O}(S^2A\sqrt{V_*H^3}/\epsilon^2\delta)$. Here, $S$ represents the number of states, $A$ the number of actions, $H$ the horizon length, $V_*$ the optimal value function, $\epsilon$ the approximation error tolerance, and $\delta$ the failure probability.

This paper investigates the 1-D hyperbolic-degenerate heat equation featuring specific boundary conditions on both the endpoint and an internal singular point. By utilizing a Carleman estimate, we demonstrate in the introduction that the system's solution semigroup is not only compact (discrete spectrum) but also exhibits logarithmically convex behavior, indicating hyperbolic properties. Consequently, we establish $L^2$-optimal control strategies for this system.

Identifying when a test sample is unfamiliar is a critical challenge with far-reaching implications for safety and reliability. This study conducts a comprehensive analysis of the current state of research on identifying shifted-out-of-distribution (Shift-OOD) instances. We categorize detection strategies into two primary categories: intrinsic methods, which evaluate uncertainty, and extrinsic methods, which utilize classification or clustering on distant data. Although intrinsic approaches excel at natural OOD shifts, extrinsic methods often surpass them in domain-specific scenarios. Furthermore, we examine the impact of various training data configurations and shift severities, noting that most intrinsic models struggle with data from their training sets yet succeed with completely new distributions. Finally, we survey promising future directions for advancing Shift-OOD detection.

We introduce and examine a quantum model of a single-molecule motor, demonstrating that electric currents drive and regulate this artificial system. In this setup, a rotator is coupled to a substrate via four tunnel sites, allowing the flow of current through the lead atoms to induce continuous rotational motion of the rotator. Furthermore, by applying a suitable potential to the tunnel sites, a current-biased motor can be realized. The study also outlines the construction of a current-controlled motor with a switchable direction of rotation. Additionally, the paper presents a current-driven dual-motor configuration, where two motors are linked by tunnel atoms to function as a coupled pair. The work concludes by addressing the integration of these molecular components into future nanoscale devices.

Origin semantics for transducers were formalized in the 1990s to address computational challenges involving the synchronized movement of both input and output. Despite nearly three decades, fundamental decision problems regarding this model remained unresolved. This paper addresses that gap by investigating two distinct semantic frameworks: origin semantics and classical semantics. For origin semantics, we contrast the decidability of language equivalence and reduction across these two types, noting that while equivalence is decidable for origin-semantics languages, it becomes undecable under reduction. Conversely, for classical semantics, both equivalence and reduction are undecable. A significant aspect of this work is a comparison of these undecability proofs, highlighting a shared reliance on a language pair where one member is context-free within each specific semantics, thereby establishing undecability for both problems regardless of the model used.

This paper investigates the f-Convolution problem, which involves computing the f-convolution of two n-element functions with a target complexity of $o(n^d)$ for a specific dimension $d$, where a brute-force method incurs $n^{2d}$ cost. We present a general technique applicable to any commutative and associative operation (such as addition or bitwise XOR) capable of achieving this goal for functions mapping to a ring of size $s \geq n^d$. Our methodology leverages four fundamental properties of the combining operation to establish a convolution theorem for $f$-convolutions and a corresponding fast algorithm with $\min\{n^d, n^{2d} \cdot \text{cost of computing } f(x,y)\}$ complexity. Specifically for the case of $f$-convolution using addition, we derive algorithms with $O(\min\{n^d, n^{2d}\} \log n)$ time complexity and demonstrate their efficacy by resolving the $f$-convolution problem for quaternions in dimensions 3 and 2, as well as for $k$-tuples under vector addition in $d$ and for $d$.

This study presents the most comprehensive spectral analysis to date of the exoplanet GJ 229B, a system renowned for its pioneering direct imaging and characterization efforts. Leveraging high-resolution (R > 100,000) near-infrared (1.0–2.5 $\mu$m) and optical (0.42–0.50 $\mu$m) data, we performed a 1D spectroscopic retrieval to derive the exoplanet's atmospheric parameters. Our findings indicate a mass of 25 M$_{\mathrm{Jup}}$ and an effective temperature of 650 K for GJ 229B. Atmospheric composition is modeled with a mean molecular weight of 2.35 (corresponding to a hydrogen-helium mixture), which aligns with the heavier element abundances inferred from previous 3D global atmospheric models. Our model successfully reproduces the broad-band photometry of the system, including data from the Spitzer Space Telescope. Furthermore, we identify specific molecular features in the retrieved profile that match the predictions of *ab initio* calculations for CH$_4$, NH$_3$, and H$_2$O.

By employing the QCD sum rules framework, we have investigated the $0^{++}$ hybrid candidate $X(1950)$. Our analysis reveals that $X(1950)$ cannot serve as a hybrid quark-gluon bound state, as it fails to align with the predicted QCD spectral function for the $0^{++}$ channel. Specifically, we found that the mass of the hybrid state $X_{hybrid}(1950)$ lies below 2 GeV, a conclusion indicating that the physical mass of $X_{hybrid}(1950)$ exceeds 2 GeV and thus excludes the possibility of its existence as a candidate within the observed mass window.

This document presents an updated measurement of the mixing-induced $C\!P$-violating phase $\phi_{s}$ and the decay width difference $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ for $B^{0}_{d}$–$B^{0}_{s}$ oscillations, derived from analyses of $3.0\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ of $pp$ collision data collected by the LHCb apparatus. The observables were determined utilizing time-integrated techniques through the analysis of $\bar{B}^{0}\to J/\psi(e^{+}e^{-})\bar{B}^{0}$ and $\bar{B}^{0}\to D^{+}K^{-}$ decays.

Airborne viruses suspended in virus-carrying aerosols can linger in enclosed environments, posing a risk of transmission through inhalation. This study presents a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) framework to model the movement of these aerosols, incorporating the effects of mechanical ventilation, human breathing, and turbulence. The study compares CFD simulations with experimental data to determine the concentration profiles of the virus-laden aerosols. The ultimate goal is to utilize these models for predicting transmission risks and formulating strategies to mitigate airborne viral spread.

The $ eta$-decay characteristics of $^{134}$Ce have been investigated through a combination of large-scale shell-model computations and experimental measurements. Theoretical predictions for the $ eta$-decay half-life, derived from shell-model matrix elements for unique single-particle transitions, align well with experimental observations. Additionally, calculated relative intensities for allowed $\gamma$-rays associated with the decay show good agreement with measured values. These findings substantiate the conclusion that the shell-model approach effectively captures the nuclear structure of $^{134}$Ce.

Double-sided auctions, prevalent in financial markets, facilitate matching supply and demand for goods and services through automated negotiation of trade prices and volumes. Although current implementations primarily address single-quantity orders, this paper extends the model to support arbitrary quantity transactions. Our proposed matching algorithm prioritizes maximizing social welfare while ensuring fiscal efficiency. To achieve this, we formulate the problem using side constraints represented as mixed integer linear programs (MILP) and demonstrate its applicability beyond financial sectors.

We investigate $F$-wave bottom mesons using the heavy quark effective theory (HQET) alongside the $P$-spin symmetry framework. By applying the predicted spin-orbit coupling patterns, we analyze the mass spectra of bottom $b$-baryons and mesons to determine the spin-orbit coupling coefficient. This study also explores the lifetimes of $F$-wave bottom bottom $b$-baryons and $B$-b mesons. Our findings indicate that the spin-orbit coupling constant is approximately $-10$ MeV, implying that $B_{1}$ and $B_{1c}$ masses are roughly $10$ MeV lower than previously reported. Furthermore, we observe that the lifetimes of $B$-baryons are generally shorter than those of $B$-b mesons, with the exception of $B_{1c}$, which exhibits a longer lifetime.

This paper investigates the dynamics of periodic configurations governed by a locally finite, translation-invariant rule on the full shift over $\mathbb{Z}^d$, with a focus on one-dimensional cases ($d=1$). It establishes that every such system possesses a nonexpansive line, defined as a line where the $L^1$-distance between image points does not exceed the distance between their corresponding source points. The authors demonstrate how the existence of this line enables the decomposition of the rule's action into parallel isometries occurring on a line and a contracting map applied to the surrounding space. Additionally, in the context of one dimension, they prove the always presence of a subset of configurations homeomorphic to the Cantor set, which remains invariant under the rule and exhibits the property of being a set of low complexity.

The rapid growth of data-driven systems has generated a substantial volume of diverse datasets, posing significant challenges for dynamical system modeling. This paper introduces a novel approach to characterize and build reduced-order models (ROMs) for such systems by leveraging machine learning techniques on latent variables that capture the essential features of the data. The study addresses three primary hurdles: (i) the high dimensionality and heterogeneity of raw data, (ii) the difficulty of defining a coordinate system for cloud-based, data-centric information, and (iii) the need to establish meaningful connections between these data points and established dynamical system theories. To achieve this, we develop a data-driven, time-stepped, and time-consistent latent dynamical system capable of generating accurate latent-time evolutions. We validate the methodology using both synthetic examples and real-world applications involving the creation of data-based ROMs.

Chess is a game of immense complexity, primarily due to the vast number of possible moves; even grandmasters often fall prey to suboptimal openings because of this depth. To address this challenge, we introduce a relatedness network of chess openings that leverages a game similarity metric to suggest the best subsequent moves for any given opening. By applying this relatedness network, we help users select superior openings and accelerate learning. Additionally, we examine the intrinsic characteristics of this relatedness structure. Empirical results indicate that utilizing this network boosts similar results for grandmasters, improves the performance of chess engines, and enhances user experiences.

This study investigates key observational features of millisecond pulsars (MSPs)—including spin periods, companion masses, and magnetic fields—to explore the accretion disk instability model (ADIM) as a primary formation mechanism. We specifically examine the mass distribution of companions for both AMHerX binary systems and isolated millisecond pulsars (IMSPs). Our findings indicate that the companion mass function for AMHerX binaries aligns with a log-normal distribution centered at approximately 0.2 solar masses ($M_\odot$), whereas IMSPs exhibit a companion mass function peaked near $0.4 M_\odot$. These distributions suggest distinct accretion disk temperatures during formation, with AMHerX binaries forming around $10^6$ K and IMSPs around $2 \times 10^6$ K, consistent with predictions from the ADIM. Furthermore, we analyze the magnetic field evolution of formed MSPs, demonstrating that the observed log-normal distribution of magnetic fields in the AMHerX population is a direct result of the accretion process.

This article examines dissipative mechanical systems that admit nonlocal constants of motion, deriving parameter estimates and establishing the conditions for the existence of global solutions. Furthermore, we present several concrete examples to illustrate these theoretical findings.

This study introduces a novel approach to 3D model retrieval via air-doodling in a VR setting, utilizing air gestures to create depth maps. Users wear a head-mounted display and interact using handheld controllers, performing depth estimation by analyzing the motion of their virtual hands. This process leverages a 3D reconstruction technique based on parallax, derived from comparing hand positions across multiple viewpoints. To facilitate this, a new coordinate system is established relative to the virtual hands, and the system infers depth by tracking hand movements across frames. The resulting hand motion depth maps are then employed for 3D object search, functioning similarly to free-form sketching. A key advantage of this air-depth-doodling technique is its ability to enable rapid, gesture-based drawing without physical contact, allowing for quick depth estimation.

This study examines the habitability of exoplanets within the habitable zone of M-dwarf stars, focusing on those with high eccentricities. We demonstrate that such planets experience significant fluctuations in received stellar flux, which can lead to diverse climate states and habitability outcomes. By utilizing the analytic eccentricity model proposed by Leconte et al. (2013), we quantify variations in insolation, temperature, and the extent of the habitable zone. Our analysis indicates that the habitable zone for eccentric exoplanets is fragmented, comprising a permanent temperate zone near the periastron, a permanently cold area at apastron, and a transitional region subject to varying thermal conditions. We further develop an analytical framework to determine the width of this intermediate zone, showing it is governed by the planet's radiative relaxation timescale and its orbital parameters. Ultimately, we argue that the distinct climate dynamics and habitability profiles of eccentric orbits demand dedicated investigation to enhance our understanding of exoplanetary systems.

This study examines the relativistic gravitational collapse of a perfect fluid sphere within an anisotropic setting, governed by a general, compatible, and divergence-free equatio of state. Starting from the underlying field equations, a system of partial differential equations (PDEs) is derived. Compatibility between the PDEs and the associated metric is established by enforcing its homogeneity. Consequently, a specific class of inhomogeneous, anisotropic, and anisotropy-free (homogeneous) cosmological models is constructed. The physical characteristics of these solutions are analyzed in detail. Furthermore, the validity of the proposed models is reinforced by comparing their predicted behavior against observational data.

We investigate the variations in black hole extremality caused by the addition of infinitesimal amounts of energy and charge. Our findings demonstrate that resulting changes in entropy stem from either a violation of local energy conditions or irreversible quantum effects. Specifically, if energy conditions hold and both quantum field states are static while remaining arbitrarily close to the black hole, the entropic change must be treated as semi-classical. In this required Chakraborty-Engelhardt-Isham-Wallden (CIIW) framework, we derive an updated first law of black hole mechanics that accounts for higher-derivative contributions to gravity. Furthermore, we examine how corrections to charged black hole charge-to-entropy ratios align with or diverge from those observed in extremality for non-Abelian gauge theories of gravity.

In reinforcement learning (RL) for goal-directed motor learning, end-effective forces (or torques) applied by a controller are often generated to maximize a reward function contingent on the robot's state. A prevalent strategy involves using an inverse dynamics model (IDM) to map these forces to joint velocities, integrating them over time, and then displacing the robot's state accordingly. This paper argues that such an approach is fundamentally flawed because numerically integrating velocities to derive positions introduces significant errors, particularly when the time steps are not sufficiently small. We propose a revised method that maps forces directly to integrated position changes, bypassing the intermediate velocity step. This new technique is demonstrated within a IDM-based RL context, where idiosyncratic dynamics allow for efficient learning of a hopping task across various simulated robots.

We extend the three-dimensional Poincaré algebra to incorporate a colour symmetry factor, creating an associated graded algebra structured over complex numbers with finite-dimensional complex Lie group representations of the associated compact type. Generalised versions of the three-dimensional Lorentz and translation generators are defined through their respective matrix representations, including specific generalised versions of the three-dimensional Lorentz and translation generators, as well as generalised versions of the three-dimensional Lorentz and translation generators, as well as generalised versions of the three-dimensional Lorentz and translation generators. Generalised versions of the three-dimensional Lorentz and translation generators are defined through their

We introduce an algorithm that generates a specific type of directed acyclic graph drawing, known as upward planar, which avoids edge crossings and aligns with a given decomposition into bidirected cycles called a bi-decomposition. This type of structure is also referred to as a 2-decomposition. Our method produces a drawing where all cycles in the bi-decomposition appear as simple, closed curves. Since any DAG can be transformed into one featuring only two source nodes via a bi-decomposition, our results imply a source of planarity.

Image-goal navigation involves directing an agent to reach a destination defined by an provided image. Although current methods have made significant strides, they often falter when facing unfamiliar environments or when interpreting complex images containing multiple objects and scenes. To address these limitations, we introduce MemoNav, a two-part framework designed to enhance both goal comprehension and instruction following. First, a temporary memory mechanism supports goal understanding, allowing the agent to retain information about previously visited locations and encountered items to form a coherent history. Second, a dedicated memory faculty enables the storage of novel navigation strategies, which are triggered by the visual goals. We evaluate our approach on two datasets: the standard 3D navigation benchmark, Memory, and a newly developed 2D benchmark, MemoNav-Goal. Results indicate that the agent's performance improves substantially on both datasets when compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

The demand for spectrum is escalating rapidly, driven by emerging applications like autonomous driving and smart cities that exceed the capacity provided by conventional cellular networks. To address this scarcity, unlicensed spectrum sharing has emerged as a promising solution. In this paper, we examine a cognitive radio scenario where a secondary network utilizes the spectrum of a primary network. The secondary base station (SBS) dynamically adjusts its transmit power to maximize its own data rate while strictly adhering to primary user (PU) interference limits. This SBS power allocation problem is non-convex; however, by introducing a specific constraint, we transform it into a convex form. We subsequently employ the successive convex approximation (SCA) method to iteratively determine an optimal power allocation strategy. The resulting algorithm is easy to implement, computationally efficient, and guarantees convergence. Finally, numerical results demonstrate that our proposed scheme outperforms existing methods in secondary network performance while effectively protecting primary users from excessive interference.

This article introduces a new approach for addressing systems with interaction constraints by utilizing hypergraphs to depict both the specific nature of connection points and the dynamics of the interaction itself. The proposed framework is utilized to demonstrate the capability of achieving global synchronization within a set of coupled oscillators.

We investigate the universal features of operator growth in Lie symmetry systems, focusing on how Lie symmetry constrains the entanglement properties of many-body wavefunctions and consequently dictates the evolution of operator entanglement. Our findings regarding late-time behavior are validated through precise computations of early-time dynamics, supported by numerical simulations.

The direct decay ratio of the Hoyle state to $^8$Be($2^+$_1\)+$\alpha$ serves as a critical indicator for understanding its structural nature as an $\alpha$-condensate. This study presents the first measurement of this decay ratio, yielding a value of $(1.0 \pm 0.4) \times 10^{-3}$, which stands as the most precise result to date. The data were obtained by irradiating a $^7$Li target with $^4$He ions at an energy of 2.95 MeV. The resulting precision enables meaningful comparisons with various theoretical models, including $\alpha$-cluster frameworks.

Dynamic fracture mechanics has recently advanced through numerical simulations, analytical models, and experiments, revealing complex behaviors such as transverse and oscillatory crack instabilities. This study investigates 2D brittle materials using a cohesive zone model to analyze oscillatory cracks at high propagation speeds. We demonstrate that when the material is isotropic, the crack's trajectory is governed primarily by propagation velocity and cohesive zone size, with oscillation amplitude scaling as $1/v$. Conversely, for anisotropic materials, material orientation becomes a decisive factor in the crack path. By examining both brittle and mixed-mode propagation, we find that oscillatory cracks emerge from a resonant interaction between the crack tip and the elastic wave field surrounding it.

This paper introduces a novel approach to calculating the feedback capacity of a specific class of finite-state channels (FSCs), termed "one-step." We establish that the feedback capacity of a one-step FSC is equivalent to the capacity of an associated single-shot channel. To achieve this, we utilize a specialized encoding strategy involving optimal control policies on control states. Furthermore, we demonstrate that computing this capacity is tractable, as it reduces to solving a convex problem. These findings significantly expand the scope of FSCs for which feedback capacity can be exactly determined, encompassing models with limited causal information regarding channel states and channel outputs with feedback. Notably, this framework covers the discrete feedback capacity of Markovian noise channels. Ultimately, we derive a closed-form formula for the feedback capacity of one-step channels with an identity input-output mapping, effectively generalizing the result previously obtained by Ostendorf et al. for control states with Gaussian transitions.

This study examines spin-triplet superconductivity within a 1D system composed of a charged quasiparticle interacting with static impurities under the influence of a Zeeman magnetic field and Rashba spin-orbit coupling. By applying a Schrodinger equation approach, we derive an exact analytical expression for the pairing interaction, identifying a finite region of parameter space where stable triplet pairing occurs. Our findings reveal that impurity-driven superconductivity is most pronounced at the point of a quantum phase transition, specifically involving the transition from the unitary to the non-unitary scattering regime. Additionally, we find that varying the relative magnitudes of the Zeeman field and spin-orbit coupling strengths can induce a superconductor-normal state transition.

The rapid expansion of tabular data across domains like healthcare and finance has spurred growing interest in using such data for natural language processing (TAPL). However, the challenges inherent in combining text and tables remain largely unaddressed. This paper introduces FTablE, a comprehensive framework evaluating factual statements involving both tabular content and natural language. To effectively assess the truthfulness of these claims, we propose two specialized sub-tasks: (1) identifying whether a claim relies on specific cells within a table, and (2) determining if a claim is supported by that identified evidence. Our framework includes an annotated dataset with over 10,000 examples drawn from diverse sources and offers two novel models designed to synthesize information from tabular data and text.

This investigation explores the essential role of complex numbers in Quantum Mechanics. We examine prominent real-valued formulations, specifically the work of Wigner, Villars, and Bolyai, with the aim of evaluating their conceptual coherence and practical applicability.

A set $R$ within a connected, simple, and undirected graph $G$ is termed *resolving* when the metric vectors formed by all vertices in $G$ relative to $R$ are distinct. The **resolving dimension** (or **metric dimension, $\beta(G)$**) of a graph $G$ is defined as the smallest possible size of such a resolving set. A graph $G$ is classified as **$k$-PPT** (or $k$-resolvable by parity testing) precisely when there exists a resolving set $R$ of cardinality $k$ such that for every vertex $v$ in $G$, the sum of the distances from $v$ to all elements within $R$ is even. In this paper, we investigate $k$-PPT properties specifically for **$2$-PPT** graphs. Our findings include:
*   Determining the necessary and sufficient criteria under which **cyclic graphs** and **complete bipartite graphs** are $2$-PPT.
*   Demonstrating that **$2$-PPT** **star graphs** must possess an even number of vertices.
*   Establishing that **$2$-PPT** **complete graphs** contain exactly **two** distinct metric dimensions (or more precisely, the property holds or fails based on structural constraints, though the original implies existence conditions).
