We investigate the asymptotic behavior of the parities of the cardinalities of specific subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ derived from irrational rotations. By applying an approach inspired by analytic number theory—originally proposed by Z. Dvo\v{r}\'ak and P. Vojt\'asht—we establish sufficient criteria for a given irrational number $\alpha$ that ensure the parity of these set cardinalities is evenly distributed. Our results notably cover both the Golden Mean and the modular inverse of any integer greater than one. Additionally, we detail the implementation of this method, illustrating how it can be extended to address a broader class of combinatorial problems.

We demonstrate that local complete intersection $k$-rational singularities exhibit the $k$-Du Bois property, while for hypersurfaces, $k$-rationality is characterized by the equivalence of the statements regarding $k$-Du Bois conditions and the vanishing of Ext groups.

This study investigates the emergence of weak antiferromagnetic long-range order in quasi-two-dimensional Heisenberg systems characterized by distinct interlayer anisotropy. We demonstrate that for sufficiently low interlayer coupling, distinct to the case of uniform coupling, the system exhibits Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) critical behavior within each two-dimensional plane. Specifically, we derive an effective model of anisotropic weakly coupled planes to evaluate the degree of anisotolerance of this BKT behavior. Our findings reveal that significant BKT characteristics persist in layers with weakly coupled Heisenberg planes even when spin anisotropy is substantial. This conclusion is supported by Monte Carlo simulations of the $O(3)$ $\sigma$-model, which involve coupled $O(3)$ symmetric planes separated by weakly coupled antiferromagnetic links.

The $a$U MSM framework, a recently introduced four-scalar extension of the Standard Model, offers a compelling solution to the strong CP problem, electroweak symmetry breaking, and dark matter existence. This model posits two primary dark matter production mechanisms: (i) the standard annihilation of stable, neutral dark matter scalars into Higgs bosons, and (ii) the resonant creation via a dark scalar mediator. This study investigates the implications of these mechanisms for dark matter abundance, utilizing current LHC data, Higgs properties from flavor observables, and the characteristics of the dark sector. Our analysis indicates that while the conventional production scenario is largely excluded by existing constraints, the resonant mechanism remains viable. Specifically, the model predicts a significant signature for dark matter detection through direct scattering experiments, alongside a substantial production rate for dark sector states at high-luminosity electron-positron colliders.

The stabilizer rank $\chi$ of a pure quantum state quantifies the distance from the state to the set of fully separable states, serving as a lower bound on the qubits required for non-stabilizer resources. This paper improves the previously established linear lower bound for the stabilizer rank of $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$ by demonstrating that $\chi \geq 2^{0.93m}$. Additionally, we derive a lower bound of $\geq \alpha^m$ for the stabilizer rank of $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$ where $\alpha > 2$ holds for all $m \geq 4$.

This study examines the behavior of the fractional energy density within a Lambda-CDM universe modeled using the Tsallis Hubble parameter law. Our analysis reveals that a real universe cannot exist when the Tsallis parameter $\tau$ is less than 1. Consequently, we investigate the case where $\tau$ exceeds 1 by employing various sub-Hubble laws to determine the fractional energy density. Our findings indicate that all such models produce a positive fractional energy density, with the specific outcome depending on the chosen sub-Hubble law. Furthermore, we explore the implications of the equation of state parameter, $w$, demonstrating that these models exhibit phantom-like characteristics when $w$ falls below -1.

The LAMBOOST Large Sky Survey Area Spectroscopic Instrument (LAMBOOST) has been operational since 2014, and this report details the characteristics of its low-resolution spectra. Our analysis indicates that approximately 90% of the 400+ million spectra collected possess a signal-to-noise ratio exceeding 10. We also examine the temporal evolution of spectral signal-to-noise, the distribution of flux calibration residuals, and the correlation between signal quality and exposure duration. Furthermore, the study assesses the impact of various data reduction parameters on the overall quality of the processed spectra.

This paper introduces an SRAM-based True Random Number Generator (TRNG) designed to overcome the vulnerabilities found in earlier SRAM implementations. Unlike previous models, this design mitigates the impact of process variations and eliminates the need for an external entropy source by utilizing the metastable states of SRAM cells. The proposed architecture leverages the latch-like behavior of these cells, using power-on transitions between 0 and 1 to generate entropy. The resulting TRNG is simple, cost-effective, and easy to fabricate. Experimental validation using 65nm, 90nm, and 180nm commercial standard-cell libraries confirms that the design yields random bits with high entropy. The study also examines the influence of circuit parameters on the output quality, demonstrating the robustness of this Sram-based approach across diverse operating conditions.

Molecular resistive switches have garnered significant attention for their potential to enable ultra-dense nonvolatile memory and neuromorphic computing systems. This study introduces a theoretical analysis of the nonlinear I-V characteristics observed in atomistic Au-thiolate-Au junctions capable of resistive switching, utilizing a model that integrates a single-electron tunneling rate with a barrier height modulated by junction electrical energy. Our analysis indicates that junctions containing fewer than 10 molecular units function as electrical nano-wires with a length under 10 nm, a feature that can be exploited to miniaturize resistive memory arrays and neuromorphic circuitry to extreme scales. Furthermore, we propose that the observed switching behavior stems from a transition between a high-resistance state, characterized by junctions with a large Poissonian distribution of single-molecule gaps, and a low-resistance state, defined by a narrow gap distribution around the mean molecular count. These findings offer a robust framework for understanding the nonlocal resistive switching mechanisms in molecular systems and guide the strategic design of high-performance molecular memory and neuromorphic devices.

Loop-Tree Diagram duality (LTD), or Loop-Tree Dualities, serves as an innovative approach to calculating multi-loop scattering amplitudes numerically, specifically converting general one-loop box integrands into a linear combination of simpler four-parton tree-level integrands. These resulting integrands exhibit enhanced integrability, thereby facilitating the direct evaluation of their contributions to the final amplitude through straightforward methods. This study extends Loop-Tree Diagram duality to scenarios involving multiple loops acting upon the same particle line. We demonstrate that applying the method to a canonical two-loop figure-eight topology yields a representation as a sum over straightforward one-loop tree-like integrands.

This paper derives eigenfunction expansion formulas for a specific category of 2-state quantum walks. We begin by summarizing the necessary conditions for a self-adjoint unitary quantum walk and subsequently present the formulas. A key application of these formulas is determining the significance of the spectral measure associated with initial states.

We examine the structure of cold, dense, and rotating stars formed from interacting layers of hadronic and gaseous (non-chiral) u, d, s quarks. Our analysis relies on the MIT bag model for the interior quark equation of state and the relativistic Hadron-Dihadron model for the hadronic phase. We construct a unified phase diagram of temperature versus chemical potential, incorporating one or more phase transition points between the hadronic and star-quark phases. By applying the maximum allowable mass constraint for such hybrid stars—determined to be $M_{\rm max} \leqslant 2.16\,M_\odot$—we derive an upper limit for the critical energy density, $\varepsilon_{\rm crit} \lesssim (145\text{--}165)\,\rm MeV/fm^3$. This value is notably lower than the $\varepsilon_{\rm crit} \approx 180\,\rm MeV/fm^3$ predicted by perturbative QCD, suggesting that the onset of the star-quark phase may occur at densities achievable within neutron stars.

We investigate the thermodynamics of a $q$-deformed Jaynes-Cummings model within the undeformed limit ($q=1$) of an $q$-deformed Rabi model, focusing on its interaction with a single undeformed quantum mechanical oscillator. Our analysis examines how the $q$-deformation influences phase transitions in the system, revealing that while it impacts the nature of the transition, it does not induce transitions in the absence of interaction (i.e., when the coupling constant is zero). Additionally, we explore the thermodynamic properties of mean energy, specific heat, entropy, and the various Stokes and anti-Stokes sidebands associated with the Rabi frequency and oscillator. Our findings indicate that $q$-deformation significantly alters these quantities, with specific heat displaying remarkable features such as $\delta$-function singularities that mark second-order phase transitions.

This study investigates Two-Rotor systems featuring a finite, classically modeled N-particle body connected via a single hinge. The authors analyze the three-dimensional rotational states of these composite objects, focusing on their energy levels and transition rates. The research demonstrates that specific localized body configurations give rise to \textit{R-negative} scissors states, representing the quantum analogues of their classical counterparts. Furthermore, the authors derive analytical formulas to compute the moments of inertia for both two-dimensional and three-dimensional classical bodies. Finally, the implications of the quantization of moments of inertia on the rotational dynamics of N-particle objects are discussed.

Transition metal oxides are renowned for their complex electronic and magnetic characteristics, which are heavily influenced by electron-electron repulsion and the interplay between kinetic energy and lattice interactions. While bulk properties have been thoroughly investigated, reducing these materials to atomic-scale thin films can trigger novel phenomena arising from dimensionality constraints and surface effects. Specifically, reducing metallic transition metal oxides to ultra-thin films often results in a phase transition to a correlated insulating state. This study examines the growth of epitaxial SrTiO$_3$-substrated La$_{0.67}$Ca$_{0.33}$MnO$_3$ (LCO) films, a perovskite structure known for its strong electron-electron and electron-phonone coupling. Using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), we analyze the valence band structure of LCO films of varying thicknesses down to approximately 5 unit cells. Our findings reveal that the metallic bulk behavior transforms into an insulating state in films as thin as 5 unit cells, a change corroborated by the emergence of a lower Hubbard band indicative of strong correlations. Furthermore, the insulating nature of these thin films is attributed to the passivation of Mn$^{3+}$-O$_{2p}$ metallic states through the formation of Mn$^{4+}$-O$_{2p}$ bonds at the SrTiO$_3$/LCO interfaces.

Diffusion of particles through disordered media is a prevalent natural occurrence, yet standard theories often fail to account for diffusion rates that are either significantly slower or faster than typical. This work examines mean-field models of discrete systems where transport is restricted by the presence of obstacles. We demonstrate that in dimensions greater than one, the interplay between transport mechanisms and the minimization of potential energy can induce "anomalous" diffusion—defined as transport that deviates from standard Brownian behavior—and simultaneously result in phase transitions. Specifically, the diffusion coefficient becomes dependent on the exponent characterizing the distribution of disordered media. Our findings are validated through simulations across diverse scenarios, including pure random environments, potential landscapes shaped like power laws, and configurations resembling percolation clusters.

This study examines the high-order statistical dependencies within cryptocurrency price movements, revealing that the network structure defined by these dependencies is stable over time. We observe that stablecoins occupy central positions in this network, whereas the degree centrality of other cryptocurrencies fluctuates significantly. Furthermore, the network's structural properties align more closely with a scale-free model than with one predicting exponential node degree distribution. These findings suggest that individual cryptocurrency returns exhibit higher-order correlations, necessitating investment strategies that account for these complex linkages.

Clouds are essential to Earth's climate, yet their formation and evolution remain poorly understood. Cloud droplets emerge from water vapor condensing onto cloud condensation nuclei (CCN), which are minute atmospheric particles. These droplets act as tracers for aerosols, which eventually become precipitation. Consequently, the concentration and characteristics of CCN significantly influence cloud and precipitation systems, as well as climate and weather patterns. This study introduces a new, efficient method to simulate CCN dynamics within atmospheric models. The approach is based on a droplet activation framework originally designed for pristine (clean) atmospheric conditions. By adapting this mechanism for use in both droplet-resolving and droplet-parameterized global models, the work provides a comprehensive analysis of the CCN number, mass, and radius distributions.

This paper introduces the concept of a compact observation space, defined as an observation space whose associated measurement space is totally bounded. We demonstrate that the space of all continuous linear maps from a Hilbert space to the observation space, equipped with the operator norm, forms a compact metric space. Subsequently, the definition of a pair of complementary compact observation spaces is proposed; such a pair ensures that the resulting combined measurement space is complete. These theoretical constructs find application in the formulation of the Dirac-Feshcochco projection method within the framework of infinite-dimensional observation spaces. Specifically, the authors define the notion of a "compact observation pair" and prove the relevant theorem regarding the compactness of the operator space. Finally, the authors apply these results to develop the Dirac-Feshcochco projection method, showing that when using complementary compact observation pairs, the method yields well-defined, unique projections.

In this study, we investigate the influence of temperature gradients and gravitational fields on electronic transport within solid systems. Specifically, we examine how variations in gravitational potential modulate both transverse energy and particle flows, demonstrating that gradients in the gravitational field can generate transverse currents. Furthermore, we analyze the role of electron-electron interactions, noting their significant impact on the magnitude of these observed phenomena.

Recent research indicates that deep learning models often exhibit "double descent" in generalization error, a phenomenon where increasing model capacity can initially improve performance before it declines again. This paper explores the concept of geometric complexity to understand such non-monotical behaviors in the generalization accuracy of models with fixed capacities. We define geometric complexity as the count of distinct data subsets that a model can separate, noting its value remains stable or decreases throughout training despite the model's internal parameters fluctuating. By leveraging this metric, we can predict whether a specific dataset will yield improved or degraded accuracy as training continues. Additionally, we demonstrate a direct correlation between geometric complexity and the sharpness of the generalization error landscape; lower geometric complexity corresponds to flatter areas that favor better generalization. These findings offer crucial insights for guiding the selection of appropriate model capacities and for developing more effective training protocols.

We present a comprehensive analysis of rare $b\to s$ decays, specifically focusing on the branching ratios for $b\to s\gamma$, $b\to s e^+e^-$, and $b\to s\mu^+\mu^-$. By employing the effective field theory framework, we determine these rates as functions of Wilson coefficients and the scale of new physics. Our study demonstrates that data from $b\to s\gamma$, $b\to s e^+e^-$, and $b\to s\mu^+\mu^- $ provide robust constraints on the parameter space defined by the relevant Wilson coefficients, thereby offering significant restrictions on theories involving physics beyond the Standard Model.

Automated Essay Scoring (AES) involves ranking essays based on their quality, a domain that attracts significant interest from Natural Language Processing (NLP) researchers. While prior work has explored various techniques to improve scoring models, Transformer architectures remain a dominant force in NLP. This study investigates the impact of pre-trained language models—including BERT and variants such as RoBERTa—on the AES task. We observe that these models, particularly when fine-tuned, yield substantial improvements over baseline systems. Additionally, we analyze the influence of training data volume and the integration of transfer learning from similar tasks. Our findings indicate that fine-tuning pre-trained transformers with available data produces the best results, and transfer learning from related tasks offers meaningful boosts to scoring accuracy.

Chances for upward mobility through education are not uniform; they vary significantly based on family background. This study examines the extent of intergenerational transmission of educational attainment within the United States, noting that this transmission might be partially driven by the fact that higher educational opportunities are more accessible to those already predisposed to pursue academic success. To address this, the authors employ a structural equilibrium model capable of accounting for such selection effects. Their preferred model, grounded in heterogeneous preferences for schooling and partial access to higher education determined by the number of years of education parents completed, successfully replicates the observed decline in the correlation between parental and children's education over time. Furthermore, the study analyzes the impacts of two counterfactual policy interventions: a scenario where all selection advantages are eliminated and a scenario removing the financial barriers to schooling. Both simulations demonstrate substantial increases in intergenerational mobility, with the latter yielding significantly higher gains. Consequently, the findings underscore the critical importance of financing educational policies.

We demonstrate that parity symmetry dictates the exchange statistics of bosons and fermions by forcing their wavefunctions to possess defined exchange phases of $\pm 1$. This establishes the standard quantum mechanics model for identical particles through the underlying symmetry of the spatial parities of their non-identical components, thereby proving that relative exchange behavior arises solely from the parities of these parts.

We introduce a modified adaptation of RingCT for decentralized cryptocurrencies, termed "Delegated RingCT." This approach leverages stealth addresses and fully homomorphic encryption to enable users to sign transactions without exposing their private keys. By utilizing our proposed technique, users can maintain their private keys offline, thereby enhancing security. Although the signing process is no longer performed directly by the user, privacy is assured through the cryptographic properties of our modified RingCT, which prevent any leakage of information regarding the selection of the specific input transaction.

We demonstrate that if an iterative method converges for undirected Laplacian matrices, it inherently solves for broader subclasses of linear systems, including those arising from directed graphs with cycle-robust orientation and more general cases involving positive semidefinite matrices. This finding generalizes previous results by Baccelli et al. (2017) and by Miller and Nevado (2019), respectively.

This study details the first observation of triple massive gauge boson production at the LHC, achieved through proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The analysis examines final states comprising three photons, an electron-positron-photon combination, or four leptons, with an integrated luminosity of 139 fb$^{-1}$. After applying selection criteria, the measured signal yields are 1099 $\pm$ 210 (statistical) $\pm$ 100 (systematic) events for the $\gamma\gamma\gamma$ channel, 1019 $\pm$ 181(stat) $\pm$ 100(sys) events for $\gamma ee\bar{\nu}$, and 1019 $\pm$ 181(stat) $\pm$ 100(sys) events for $\gamma ee\bar{\nu}$, with no significant discrepancies observed between data and Standard Model predictions. The combined production cross-section for three massive gauge bosons stands at 1.11 $\pm$ 0.21(stat) $\pm$ 0.10(sys) mb, representing a significance of 5.2 sigma. Furthermore, differential cross-sections are examined across various kinematic distributions, and constraints on the trilinear gauge coupling parameters are derived.

Hebrew NLP has advanced significantly over the last few years, achieving state-of-the-art performance on core tasks such as tokenization, lemmatization, part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, parsing, question answering, and sentiment analysis. This paper introduces a comprehensive review of established and emerging methods, along with an analysis of key Hebrew NLP challenges. Additionally, it examines available datasets and evaluation metrics, summarizing recent achievements across major Hebrew NLP tasks to highlight current progress and directions for future research.

This study investigates isometric methods for reducing dimensionality within $L_p$ spaces. We demonstrate that for any finite set of vectors in $L_p$, maximizing functions can be approximated (within an $\varepsilon$ margin) using representations in a space of dimension roughly $\varepsilon^{-1}$ with nearly isometric properties. Specifically, this dimension is significantly lower than the standard bound required for general linear embedding, which is typically $\dim = \varepsilon^{-1}$. We further provide matching lower bounds for computational complexity, showing that any algorithm aiming for an $\varepsilon$ approximation must utilize a subspace of at least $\varepsilon^{-1}$ dimensions. We also present an algorithm that achieves this approximation in $\varepsilon^{-O(1)}$ time. These results extend previous findings by Shalev-Shwaver and Sridharan (2012), which were limited to $p=2$, covering the broader range of $1 \leq p < \infty$.

Driven by the success of artificial neural networks, machine learning has undergone significant recent growth. However, standard learning methods often lack the capacity for lifelong acquisition, leading to a phenomenon termed "catastrophic forgetting," wherein a model retains a new dataset's patterns at the expense of its previous knowledge. Overcoming this challenge is essential for "continual learning," a field that seeks to circumvent the need to keep all past data available and allows models to accumulate knowledge progressively. This study examines the relationship between generalization and the ability to keep knowledge over time. We find that the extent to which a model can generalize to unseen inputs is a key determinant in how effectively it maintains prior knowledge during sequential learning tasks. Specifically, models utilizing strong regularization to enhance generalization, such as those employing dropout, demonstrate superior performance in continual learning scenarios compared to models with weaker regularization. These insights are supported by theoretical reasoning and validated through experiments on both synthetic tasks and practical applications.

This paper introduces a novel formulation of the model predictive safety filter (MPSF) designed to enhance computational efficiency while maintaining robustness. Our approach leverages a dual-mode system consisting of a safety barrier function and a stabilizing controler. By mode switching only once at the beginning of the horizon, our method significantly cuts down on solving mixed logical dynamical (MLDs) problems compared to per-step switching, thereby ensuring the real-time capability. Furthermore, theoretical proofs confirm that this MPSF variant guarantees global stability and satisfies all system constraints. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm delivers performance nearly identical to that of the standard MPSF but with a marked improvement in calculation speed.

Real-world quantum key distribution (QKD) systems are constrained by hardware flaws, which severely limit their security against sophisticated eavesdropping strategies. To address this, recent research has focused on side-channel QKD protocols that incorporate specific side information gathered by the adversary. This work extends that research by introducing a side-channel decoy-mule protocol, a variation of the standard decoy-mule method. We demonstrate the security of this scheme under conditions where the adversary possesses complete knowledge of the legitimate parties' measurement bases and the窃听 strategy. Notably, our analysis reveals that the side information acquired by the eavesdrop does not substantially diminish the key generation rates achievable in the information-reconciliation phase.

This paper investigates how different pretraining corpora affect large-scale language model (LM) performance in in-context learning (ICL). We evaluate ICL capabilities using automatic benchmarks across tasks such as question answering, named entity recognition, and relation extraction. Our findings reveal that while generalization performance varies depending on the corpus source, there is no single ideal corpus for all scenarios. We also demonstrate that combining multiple corporas yields superior results compared to individual components. Furthermore, these results provide valuable insights for guiding future language model pretraining strategies. Our code and trained models are accessible at https://github.com/rohiishah/ICL-Corpus.

We present a comprehensive model of cold gas dynamics within galaxy clusters, covering both cloud formation and destruction. Formation occurs through gravitational instability in the cooling radiation field of the intracluster medium (ICM), while destruction arises from thermal and hydrodynamic interactions with the surrounding hot gas. Our findings indicate that cloud lifetimes are governed by the interplay between formation and destruction rates. Specifically, we demonstrate that cloud formation can offset destruction, leading to the establishment of a steady-state population of cold gas. Crucially, the existence of such a cold gas phase is not merely incidental; it is a fundamental requirement for cooling flow formation.

Investigating $B$-meson decays and $B$-baryon decays allows for predictions regarding $B$-baryon processes, as both rely on the same fundamental quark transitions. Precision measurements of these quark-flavor-changing neutral current (FCFN) and flavor-conserving neutral current (FCFN) decays are crucial for testing the Standard Model, particularly through $CP$ violation analyses. While the LHCb experiment has recently achieved significant advancements in reconstructing $B$-baryon decays, the analysis of $B$-meson decays remains a powerful tool for enhancing experimental precision.

We have identified and demonstrated duality relations among hard scattering amplitudes for $n$-point interactions in the hard limit where the momentum transfer scales as $|t| \sim 1/\alpha'$. These relations hold specifically for external states involving up to 4 bosons and any number of fermions in open superstring theory. Utilizing these dualities, we derive new duality equations applicable to hard string amplitudes with up to 10 fermions and no more than four bosons, provided the remaining particles are not specified. These findings significantly aid in constructing n-point hard string amplitudes by expressing them as linear combinations of known lower-order hard string amplitudes.

Future mobile networks will increasingly rely on network function virtualization (NFV) to support diverse, high-volume, and dynamic traffic demands. Consequently, predicting traffic patterns becomes essential for optimizing resource management in these networks. This paper presents a comprehensive approach combining deep learning for traffic forecasting with a deep reinforcement learning-based method for adaptive resource allocation. First, we employ deep learning models to forecast traffic loads, utilizing these predictions as input for our deep reinforcement learning resource management system. Second, we address the challenges of transient traffic fluctuations by leveraging load forecasting to mitigate prediction errors. Third, we utilize the deep policy gradient algorithm to maximize resource efficiency, ensuring optimal performance under varying conditions. Finally, we validate our approach through extensive simulations, comparing our deep learning forecasting models against established state-of-the-art techniques and evaluating the policy gradient model versus other deep reinforcement learning alternatives. Results indicate that our proposed framework delivers superior accuracy in traffic forecasting and enhanced precision in resource management.

Zerospeech serves as a widely utilized speech synthesis benchmark, employing HMM-based systems that construct fundamental units from phone triphones using unigram acoustic models. This paper presents a re-examination of Zerospeech using retrained models, a refined system architecture, and an improved training strategy. The study addresses the original system's suboptimal phone alignment by implementing a training protocol that leverages a large-scale speech corpus to pre-train the Zerospeech model before fine-tuning it on a specific dataset. This approach yields significantly enhanced phone alignments, which in turn boosts the quality of generated unit acoustic models. The resulting system achieves a reduction in mean square error (MSE) of 2.5 dB and a standard deviation (SD) of 1.5 dB compared to the author's original publication.

Motion planning for multi-limbed systems is heavily constrained by both dynamics and kinematics, often resulting in highly non-convex optimization challenges that lead to local minima. To mitigate this, we introduce a novel technique that smooths the differential effect of collision checks across a robot's configuration space. This approach allows for more integrated omnidirectional collision avoidance within a single optimization framework, thereby enhancing the probability of finding a valid solution. Furthermore, we establish theoretical proof regarding the differentiability of these smoothed checks and validate our methodology through simulations involving a four-legged robot.

The transition from classical resource theories to the quantum domain has been impeded by a lack of general framework for defining resource theories and determining resource orders. This study introduces a structured approach to formulating resource theories and provides a characterization of transformational orders applicable to arbitrary theories. Specifically, for affine versions, a necessary condition is established: transformation is physical only if it preserves the representability of the relevant sets of states. This preservation requirement is verified as both necessary and sufficient for specific cases, notably within resource theories based on positive operator-valued measures.

This paper investigates the motion of a pendulum suspended from a support that undergoes vertical parametric excitation. The study applies the modified averaged Lagrangian method alongside the small-angle approximation to derive approximate analytical solutions for both the short- and long-term behavior of the system's response. These findings are contrasted with results generated by a numerical integration of the full equations of movement to validate their accuracy. The research further explores how the stability of the stationary state is influenced by the frequency and amplitude of the parametric driving force.

Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD) is a prevalent technique for training machine learning models across a network of devices, yet it is vulnerable to communication failures caused by outliers or adversarial data, often resulting in degraded performance. To address this, this study introduces a novel robust framework, Distributionally Robust Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DR-DSGD), which minimizes the worst-case loss by optimizing over an $\epsilon$-ambit of distributions centered on the prior, prior knowledge. This approach effectively mitigates the impact of data distribution shifts and injected adversarial inputs. Communication efficiency is significantly enhanced by restricting the communication ambit to only the most recently aggregated gradients rather than transmitting it fully at every step. Theoretical analysis provides convergence guarantees for the DR-DSGD algorithm, which are subsequently validated through empirical results on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

We have measured energy deposition within the participant frame during high-energy nuclear collisions, utilizing the method of calculating transverse momentum ($k_T$) sums as a proxy. This measurement, conducted at the CERN Super Proton Synchrotron's CERN Synchrotron (CERN) facility with a nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 27$ TeV, covers central Pb-Pb collisions. The analyzed system involves charged particles with pseudorapidities $|\eta| < 0.8$ and transverse momenta exceeding $1$ GeV/$c$. Results indicate that the resulting energy deposition scales with the particle multiplicity generated in the participant frame, supporting the notion of particle production originating from a source with a temperature distribution.

This study investigates the role of magnetic fields in the star formation process by simulating the collapse of a magnetized Bonnor-Ebert sphere, a scenario that mirrors the early phases of star formation. We ran simulations with three distinct field strengths: zero, a moderate level ($\sim 10\,\mu$G), and a strong level ($\sim 100\,\mu$G) that prevents significant accretion onto the central protostar. The resulting jet ejection rates were quantified by analyzing the outflows' mass and momentum. Our findings indicate that a protostellar jet emerges exclusively when magnetic fields are either absent or moderately strong; excessive field strength suppresses jet formation. Furthermore, the presence of a magnetic field substantially alters the jet's morphology and internal structure. Moderate field strengths produce collimated jets featuring shock waves, whereas strong fields generate more diffuse outflows characterized by a bipolar outflow pattern.

This study addresses the problem of handling actuator saturation in nonlinear systems subject to state constraints. A novel performance safety evaluation (PSE) function is proposed to manage the balance between system performance and saturation limits. The PSE Lyapunov function ensures a specific subset of the safe set remains invariant, thereby guaranteeing safe operation. The proposed control method integrates a modified control barrier function (CBF) with an anti-windup technique. This new framework offers greater flexibility in balancing performance degradation and system saturation by leveraging the proposed PSE Lyapunov function. The overall approach ensures safe operation, safety, and ensures specific performance levels.

This study examines the resonant dynamics of the Earth's gravitational field affecting a high-area-to-mass ratio (HAMR) object within the 1:1 resonance, with a specific focus on how orbital equilibria are influenced. The analysis reveals that, unlike classical resonances, the orbital oblateness of the Earth substantially shifts the resonant equilibrium points. The paper further outlines the conditions necessary for these Hamiltonian systems to remain fully degenerate, partially degenerate, or completely non-degenerate. Finally, the authors quantify the variations in the system's degree of degeneracy as a function of the HAMR object's area-to-mass ratio.

This work examines various tight-binding (TB) frameworks for modeling optical phenomena, with a specific focus on incorporating light-matrix interactions. We analyze the transition from real-space to reciprocal-space TB representations and demonstrate that transforming the optical vector potential from velocity to dipole gauges in k-space introduces an effective site-dependent St\"uckelberg phase. Adopting the dipole gauge within tight-binding formulations proves advantageous for elucidating light-matter coupling mechanisms and yields a dynamic polarizability that aligns well with the supercell T-matrix method and finite-difference time-domain approaches.

We introduce a novel method for estimating a target object's 3D pose and shape from a single depth image by leveraging an external point cloud to handle intra-class diversity. Our approach treats this as a registration problem between the external and target point clouds, where the former is generated via 3D object detection and segmentation from the single depth image. To handle shape and appearance variations, we utilize an articulated model that treats the external cloud as a template for alignment with the target. Our strategy performs non-rigid registration to estimate pose and shape, followed by the integration of range data to refine these estimates.

This paper introduces a rejection algorithm for generating random variables following a bivariate Cauchy distribution, defined by a complex location parameter ($\delta \in \mathbb{C}$) and a complex scale parameter ($\eta \in \mathbb{C}$). While F. J. Fortescue provided the initial Cauchy density in 1934 and G. A. Givens and D. S. Greenwood later proposed an acceptance-rejection method in 1955, this study presents a novel algorithm capable of simultaneously sampling both the location and scale parameters. This approach is notably more efficient than previous methods designed solely for real-valued $\eta$ and $\delta$, which were proposed by D. J. Hand and P. J. Rousseeuigt in 1987 and by P. J. R. R. Robert in 1987.

Basket trials represent an increasingly popular design for assessing the efficacy of a novel therapy across multiple patient subgroups defined by distinct biological markers. These trials are typically structured so that interim analyses allow for independent go-or-stop decisions for each specific arm. To address this, we introduce a Bayesian framework utilizing a multivariate normal distribution to simultaneously infer treatment effects and assess markers while formally accounting for the correlation among these estimators. By leveraging the adaptive nature of basket trials, we also define a Bayesian predictive probability metric to inform future modifications to the study. Additionally, we propose an innovative multivariate ordered multivariate normal mixture prior that enhances the power to detect treatment responses, particularly in scenarios with a high number of arms showing no activity. Simulations indicate that our method possesses strong control over type I error rates and delivers accurate predictive capabilities.

The surge in demand for high-precision motion control has necessitated the adoption of advanced control strategies to overcome the limitations of conventional methods, which often struggle with parameter variations, external disturbances, and nonlinearities. Although sliding mode control (SMC) offers robustness in such challenging environments, it introduces significant chattering that degrades tracking performance and accelerates actuator wear. To mitigate this issue, this study proposes an innovative scheme integrating a fractional-order super-twisting sliding mode controller with a wavelet-based Lyapunov function-based (WLSMC). The wavelet function serves a dual purpose: it smoothes the sliding mode surface to reduce chattering and acts as an effective filter for noise and disturbances. The proposed fractional-order super-twisting SMC further reduces switching frequency while ensuring robustness against uncertainties and干扰. The validity of this new strategy is verified through comparative analyses on both simulated scenarios and a practical 1-gof rotary table, demonstrating superior results regarding steady-state error and control signal smoothness relative to existing approaches.

We introduce PRNet, an innovative keypoint and keyframe network designed for robust four-frame point cloud registration. This methodology utilizes deep learning to align misaligned spatial data sets containing between two and four instances. We begin by outlining the challenges inherent in registering point clouds through multiple keypoints and introducing a novel framework that simultaneously detects feature landmarks and performs geometric alignment. We then present a keypoint detection module capable of identifying critical features while ensuring geometric consistency, alongside a keyframe matching module that leverages these features for accurate registration. To enhance the reliability of landmark identification, we integrate a loss function enforcing geometric coherence. Furthermore, we apply self-supervised learning principles to facilitate end-to-end training without requiring ground truth alignments. Experimental results demonstrate that PRNet significantly surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches in handling multi-spatial registration tasks.

A group $G$ exhibits the property $R_\infty$ if the count of twisted conjugacy classes is infinite for every endomism of $G$. This paper investigates the $R_\infty$ behavior in the context of group extensions. Specifically, we demonstrate that certain non-trivial extensions of an $R_\infty$-group by a perfect group also possess the $R_\infty$ property. Additionally, we introduce a novel sufficient condition ensuring that specific solvable groups satisfy property $R_\infty$.

The recent measurement of the top quark mass by the Tevatron collaboration has narrowed the range of uncertainty regarding this critical parameter. Given top quark's significant influence on Higgs potential stability, this updated mass value allows for a more precise investigation into potential stability. We conduct a comprehensive analysis of this updated uncertainty, demonstrating that even with Tevatron precision, the Higgs potential remains stable. Furthermore, our findings indicate that determining the metastability-forgiveness threshold—required to confirm potential stability with greater certainty—demands top quark mass precision at the level of 250 MeV, a target achievable only through data from the High-Luminosity LHC and High Energy Colliders.

We introduce a time-resolved scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) method aimed at capturing ultrafast changes in both the topography and local density of states. The technique utilizes time-resolved data to infer the local density of states through a convolution with an unknown point spread function (PSF), employing the PSF's assumed smoothness to enforce continuity constraints that stabilize the inversion process. Validation through simulations and experimental work on the photo-induced lifting of the Kohn anomaly in photoemission spectra demonstrates that this approach successfully reconstructs hidden spectral features.

This study calculates the longitudinal and transverse light-front distribution amplitudes, along with their associated numerical outcomes, for both the $B_s^0$ and $B^0$ mesons. As a longitudinal case, the three-quark–one-heavy-quark framework is adopted, whereas a two-quark heavy-quark model underpins the transverse distribution amplitude. These derived results are utilized to evaluate the external heavy-quark moments of $c \to b$ transitions.

This study investigates the properties of the Bochner-Riesz means for the wave group on $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$, specifically focusing on the space ${\Sigma}_s^\sigma$, which consists of wave group elements with Fourier transforms supported on the light cone and belonging to the Sobolev space $H^s$. We demonstrate that if $s > \frac{n}{2}$, this space is nontrivial under the condition $\sigma \in L^{2,\gamma}$ with $\gamma > (n+1)s - n$. Additionally, we establish that the inclusion mapping from ${\Sigma}_s^\sigma$ to $H^{s-\frac{n}{p}}$ is continuous for $2 \leq p < \frac{2s}{s-n}$, which is optimal when $s > \frac{n}{2}$.

We introduce a cross-modal approach to solve the challenge of segmenting instances in unlabeled modalities that lack labels but are paired with labeled modalities of the same type. This task is essential for integrating new imaging technologies into clinical practice, as it eliminates the need for manual annotation. Although our generated synthetic data mimics structural characteristics through image transformation, current translation models fail to produce realistic content due to the complexity of anatomical structures. Additionally, segmentation models trained on translated images underperform compared to those using ground truth. To overcome these hurdles, we combine a segmentation-aware image translation model with a translation-aware instance segmentation network. Our method successfully generates high-quality translated images and achieves state-of-the-art results across multiple 3D medical applications, including cardiac nuclei, pulmonary nodules, and retinal layers.

This paper introduces a new approach to action recognition that utilizes video features as input. Our method employs Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) to create future video features, which are then used to predict the corresponding action. We present an attention-based dynamic recurrent mechanism to produce these future features, leveraging the current video feature, its preceding counterparts, and the associated motion information. This attentional dynamic rnn allows for selective focus on crucial inputs, resulting in effective action prediction. We validate our approach on two major public datasets, 2D and 3D action recognition tasks using Kinetics and HMDB51, where we outperform state-of-the-art techniques.

The search for biosignatures on exoplanets is a primary goal of current and upcoming space missions, such as the James Webb Space Telescope. Evaluating the habitability of these worlds requires a comprehensive understanding of their host stars, particularly regarding stellar flares. These events can be categorized into those emitting primarily in X-rays and ultraviolet (UV) wavelengths and those radiating in the white-light spectrum. While X-ray/UV flares are well-documented, white-light flares are relatively rare, limiting our knowledge of their characteristics. This study presents an analysis of white-light flares observed from the nearby M-dwarf Proxima Centauri using data from the PLATO mission's on-board cameras. We demonstrate that the flares detected by PLATO correlate with the more energetic X-ray/UV flares identified by X-ray telescopes, suggesting that PLATO's data can be used to constrain the frequency of high-energy flares on Proxima b. Furthermore, we find that the flares occurring in the visible spectrum are significantly more frequent than previously estimated, a finding with critical implications for determining the potential habitability of exoplanets orbiting M-dwarf stars.

An oriented 7-manifold equipped with a G₂ structure is classified as nearly parallel if its associated almost complex Sasakian structure is tight, meaning it links with real Killing spinors. In this study, we demonstrate that a nearly parallel G₂ structure on an oriented 7-manifold is affinely equivalent to a specific configuration: a metric with non-positively curved, non-trivial curvature properties, or more precisely, a metric with non-positively curved, non-trivial properties.

This work examines $C^{*}$-algebras within a complex Hilbert space setting. Initially, we provide a characterization of $C^{*}$-alge also containing normal operators. Subsequently, we present characterizations for $C^{*}$-alge that contain either commutative groups of unitary operators or collections of $C^{*}$-algebras of unitary operators, where the group is generated by a single element.

We investigate $p$-core $p'$-partitions (where $p$ and $p'$ are distinct primes) through the lens of a specialized two-dimensional coordinate system, or "frame," utilizing solely integers divisible by either $p$ or $p'$. This theoretical framework not only clarifies the structural properties of these objects but also yields a concise, bidirectional partition condition necessary and sufficient for the existence of $p$-core $p'$-partitions within specific sets of integers defined by the 2D coordinates.

Deep learning for 3D object recognition has achieved significant milestones, yet the generalizability of these networks remains constrained by training data limitations. To overcome this, we introduce a self-supervised strategy utilizing data augmentation to align 2D image and 3D depth predictions, thereby enabling object detection without explicit supervision. This approach enhances existing supervised detectors by expanding the effective capacity of training datasets. We categorize thirty-three-dimensional augmentations into three groups: local, part-based, and global transformations, with an emphasis on deriving informative instances through random selection within each category. By leveraging viewpoint predictions to guide the sampling of augmented 3D scenes, we create dense, reliable supervision signals. Experiments conducted on PointNetpp demonstrate that our method yields substantial performance gains, achieving a 3.3 percentage point increase in mAP and a 3.3 increase in mIoU on the SemanticKITTI dataset.

This study introduces a distributed, collision-free medium access protocol for FMCW radar networks operating in shared spectrum, leveraging carrier sense multiple access with collision detection (CSMA/CD). The mechanism utilizes radar range detection capabilities to identify concurrent transmissions and enforce CCA/CD functions. Following the initial presentation of the protocol, the paper provides a comprehensive performance analysis, supported by both theoretical derivations and numerical simulations. The results demonstrate the protocol's effectiveness in preventing collisions and its ability to achieve high throughput.

We investigate the interaction of entangled photons with a nanodiamond, observing the "photon echo" effect as a signature of its involvement. Our analysis of the full experimental setup, including a detailed accounting of all photon losses, demonstrates that our results remain consistent with traditional optical theories. Nevertheless, our study offers a framework for future experiments aimed at exploring genuine quantum entanglement between light and matter systems.

By viewing the $V$-line bundle over $\mathbf{C}P(V)$ as a pullback from the quotient Grassmannian $\mathbf{C}P(G)$, we derive the $K$-theoretical Chatelet surface as the equivariant $K$-theoretical group of a specific $U(1)$ principal bundle with structure group $GL(2, \mathbb{C})$.

Temporal Knowledge Graph Completion (TKGC) has emerged as a popular technique for reasoning about event and temporal data graphs. A primary challenge in TKGC is selecting an appropriate model, which requires balancing computational efficiency with expressive power. Recently, neural network-based methods have gained traction for handling TKGC tasks. This paper introduces a new neural network approach for temporal knowledge graph completion that achieves both high efficiency and robust performance. We evaluate our method against state-of-the-art techniques across multiple datasets and time-sampling intervals, demonstrating significant improvements in results. Furthermore, we analyze the method's reasoning capabilities for both regular and complex temporal rules. The source code will be made publicly available.

Rigid-body collisions generate ground vibrations that can be perceived auditorily. This research investigates the auditory detectability of such sounds in virtual environments by analyzing the acoustic implications of moving rigid agents across a simulation floor. We introduce a streamlined acoustic model that captures the physics of agent-ground impacts, enabling the generation of audible simsound. By varying in-simulation physical parameters, we determine the conditions necessary to make these simulated sounds perceptible. Our findings indicate that agent mass, velocity, and the collision stiffness coefficient are critical factors. Furthermore, we validate the simmodel against real-world microphone data, demonstrating that audible ground impacts correspond to distinct, localized spikes in the frequency spectrum.

The objective of demonstrating nonlocality through "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs, such as the original Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) argument, is to establish, with certainty in every instance, the impossibility of local realism. Previous investigations have examined how experimental imperfections impact the feasibility of these proofs when correlations are not perfectly matched to theoretical predictions. In this study, we demonstrate the viability of an "always-type" proof even with significant deviations from ideal expectations by showing that quantum mechanics remains valid under such flawed conditions. Notably, our analysis indicates that achieving the goals of the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilner (GHZ) proof does not necessitate perfectly equal joint probabilities for specific measurement outcomes; rather, it suffices to construct a proof based on imperfectly correlated scenarios.

Flat bands denote regions of the energy spectrum where the flatness of energy levels renders systems nearly non-itinerant. In moiré superlattices, these flat bands emerge from the moiré potential, which significantly lowers the band energy scale relative to the magnetic energy scale. This reduction allows quantum fluctuations to dominate, producing diverse phenomena such as superconductivity, magnetism, and topological effects. In this review, the formation mechanisms of flat bands in moiré systems are examined, alongside their interactions with magnetism and topology. Particular attention is given to the strong coupling between flat bands and itinerant electrons, which can generate moiré textures of topological structures and enable coexistence with superconductivity. Finally, the paper outlines current experimental progress and future research avenues in moiré research.

The hydrogen boride layer, Li2BH3, is a recently identified superconductor noted for its exceptional thermal stability. This study employs first-principles calculations to investigate its superconducting mechanisms. We find that the superconducting potential of Li2BH3 stems from the unique electronic structure of the E1u band, which arises from the hybridization of Li-p and B-p orbitals. Notably, the B-H bond plays a critical role in generating this specific band structure. Furthermore, we observe that Li-p and B-p hybridization is a general phenomenon in hydrogen boride layers, suggesting a promising avenue for discovering additional superconductors within this class. Finally, we derive an isotope-mass-dependent scaling exponent of approximately 0.5 for the isotope effect, underscoring the significance of hydrogen in the superconducting process.

Flattened partitions are defined as ordered sequences of positive integers where each term is at least as large as the one preceding it, derived from standard partition theory. While the count of such sequences with a given length summing to $n$ corresponds to OEIS sequence A124324, this work investigates their behavior when constrained by a maximum part size $m$. Specifically, we derive asymptotic estimates for the count of these sequences summing to $n$ with parts no larger than $m$ in two scenarios: first when $m$ is fixed, yielding an expression of order $n^{(m-1)/2}$, and second when $m$ grows to infinity with $m \sim \sqrt{\ln 2} \sqrt{m}$.

This study investigates the relationship between spectral stiffness and the stationary distribution density within the framework of ergodic theory. Specifically, we demonstrate that, given a stiffness lower bound within an appropriate functional space, any unique invariant measure for an ergodic dynamics on a compact Riemannian manifold must be a probability measure. Furthermore, under additional conditions concerning the functional type of the underlying group, the functional stiffness exponent directly dictates the lower bound of the $L^2$-decay rate associated with the heat semigroup. These findings are applied to scenarios involving the heat equation advected by stochastic flows and random wave equations.

Fail-operational systems for highly automated driving are required to execute an immediate transition to a manual takeover whenever they recognize an inability to manage the driving context. This paper investigates the necessity of architectural redundancy to guarantee such operability. Architectural elements, defined here as the computational components responsible for perception, decision-making, and actuation, are analyzed. We introduce a formal framework grounded in discrete event systems to represent both the internal states of these architectural elements and the driving context. Using this model, we determine the minimal number of independent Architectural Elements (AEs) mandated for a reliable function handover. Our findings indicate that computational subsystems handling actuation, as well as those dedicated to actuation and decision logic, must be implemented in quadruply redundant configurations, while perception and control systems can operate with triple redundancy.

Clustering serves as a fundamental technique for organizing and compressing vast datasets. In numerous real-world scenarios, such as grouping cells in single-cell RNA sequencing or individuals based on medical records, data points are not static but evolve over time. Consequently, it is crucial to account for data dynamism to fully understand the underlying system. Existing methods for dynamic data clustering often fail to adequately capture this temporal behavior or lack a rigorous theoretical basis for the time-evolution of clusters. This paper introduces a novel approach that treats clustering as a time-evolving process governed by differential equations. Our methodology is supported by a new theoretical framework grounded in the concept of "clustered trajectories," which provides the mathematical proof for our algorithms. We propose two specific algorithms, each with a guaranteed global convergence. Furthermore, our framework is versatile, capable of being adapted for various data types, including continuous and discrete signals.

Recent investigations into Leibniz's historical development of calculus have championed Leixbniz's own symbolic notation as the most authentic framework representing the New Method. In contrast, contemporary research frequently adopts William Knorr's reconstructed version of this New Method, which relies on modern mathematical concepts. This article offers a critical examination of such anachronistic approaches, arguing instead for the rigorous historical and philosophical fidelity to Leibniz's original thought. Furthermore, it introduces a novel formal system grounded in abstract algebraic semantics that captures the essence of the New Method without imposing modern mathematical structures.

We investigate the cosmological constraints achievable through HI intensity mapping (HI IM) using the CMB-S4 concept for a next-generation radio telescope. Our analysis examines how HI IM power spectrum multipoles can constrain key cosmological parameters, including $\Omega_{\rm m}$, $\Omega_{\rm b}$, $H_0$, $\sigma_8$, and $\Gamma$. We find that even the monopole and quadrupole moments from a 10-meter aperture telescope could restrict these parameters to within a few percent accuracy. Furthermore, including the hexadecapole moment is expected to significantly enhance these constraints. Our results indicate that the total bias variance in the quadrupole from a 10-meter telescope would be roughly 10 times greater than that from a 3-meter telescope, primarily due to increased shot noise. Consequently, the 3-meter telescope offers superior performance for cosmological constraints, with its total bias variance being approximately 100 times lower.

where $\mathrm{P}_{n}$ denotes the projection onto the quotient space $\mathrm{span}\{\mathbf{x}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{n}\}/\mathrm{span}\{\mathbf{x}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{n-1}\}$, and $\mathrm{vol}_{n}$ represents the $n$-dimensional volume. If

A significant challenge in recommender systems is data sparsity, which has led to considerable research into mitigating this issue through multi-task learning. Nevertheless, current multi-task approaches often indiscriminately aggregate shared representations, ignoring both the intrinsic differences between tasks and the varying relevance of shared data specific to individual tasks. To address this, we propose Share-and-Update-Devote (S.U.D.), a novel multi-task framework that utilizes task-specific data to enhance performance while accounting for their unique characteristics. Specifically, S.U.D. first extracts shared components from input representations, then generates task-differentiated representations by updating these shared structures, and finally allocates task-differentiated features back to optimize shared task-specific embeddings. Experiments conducted on diverse datasets demonstrate that S.U. outperforms state-of-the-art methods, and analysis confirms its effectiveness in capturing both the similarities and differences among tasks.

This paper investigates the asymptotic behavior of two distinct families of random matrices. The first consists of independently identically distributed (i.i.d.) matrices with a common distribution that possesses a finite fourth moment. Within this group, we determine both the limiting shape of the eigenvalue support and the probability density function governing the empirical spectral distribution (ESD), noting a convergence in distribution as the dimension grows. Furthermore, we explicitly address the case for Gaussian matrices with GEG (likely a typo for GOE, but we assume the user meant a specific ensemble or condition) structure.

The second family comprises asymptotically freely independent matrices, each uniformly distributed over the unitary orbit of a deterministic one. For these matrices, we derive results regarding their global spectral properties, including the support of the limit and the form of the limiting ESD.

Specifically, for matrices in the first group, we obtain more precise analytical results under additional assumptions. When the entries follow a Gamma distribution, we demonstrate that the empirical spectral distribution converges weakly to the Marcenko-Pastur law as the matrix size tends to infinity. Similarly, for the second group, assuming entry-wise convergence to a Gaussian distribution, we prove that the ESD of the squared matrix converges weakly to the semi-circular law in the large-size limit.

This article introduces a method for monitoring real-time systems using Metric Interval Temporal Logic (MITL). The proposed algorithm determines the closest match between a system's execution trace and a specified MITL formula, offering a measure of how much the trace deviates from compliance. The distance metric relies on a user-defined input function, enabling the detection of minimal adjustments required for the trace to satisfy the logic. The distance between a trace and the MITL formula can be computed through dynamic programming. The article further extends the approach to handle distances involving bounded future and past variants of the full MITL spectrum. The validity of these methods has been confirmed through implementation and testing on the Merlin model checker.

This study investigates meson-meson scattering within the $I=0$ channel, specifically examining $B_s^0 B^0 \to B_s^- B^+$ and $B_s^0 B_s^\pm \to B_s^\pm B_s^\mp$ ($B^\pm$ denoting $B^\mp$ with opposite charge) transitions. Our analysis reveals that isospin violation in these processes stems primarily from $c\bar{c}$ mass differences, with the strongest contributions arising from charm-quark exchange mechanisms. We find that the branching ratios for the charge-neutral $B_s^0 B^0 \to B_s^- B^+$ decay are comparable in magnitude to those of the isospin-conserving $B_s^\pm B_s^\mp \to B_s^\pm B_s^\mp$ decay, a result that stands in contrast to expectations where isospin-violating modes would be significantly suppressed.

The GRAVITY acquisition camera (GAC) serves as a vital component of the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI) at ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile. Designed to facilitate both automated and manual VLTI operations, GAC fulfills three primary functions: guiding the telescope, locking onto targets, and performing astrometric measurements. This paper details the optical architecture and performance characteristics of the GAC, with a specific focus on its imaging system. We analyze the camera's point spread function (PSF) using both physical models and high-fidelity simulations. Furthermore, we present PSF observations acquired from the GAC itself to validate our findings, comparing them against results from analytical models. These studies reveal that the camera's PSF is largely determined by the pixel size, exhibiting a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of approximately 2.5 pixels.

This study introduces an efficient parameterized approximation scheme (XPZP) for the k-Capacitated Supplier problem with the following constraints: (1) the total number of clients is limited, (2) the maximum client demand is bounded, and (3) the largest facility size does not exceed a certain threshold. Given that the problem is W1-hard under parameterization with the number of suppliers, this hardness likely precludes a fully efficient f*-hardness result. The proposed PTAS relies on a combination of continuous relaxation, the localizable rounding technique, and a specific algorithm for the related k-Capacitated Supplier problem where each client is located within distance d of a facility, with the facility's capacity reduced proportionally to the removed clients.

We examine the sequential cascading of photon releases from two-level and three-state quantum models, considering both constant and time-varying transition rates. Our analysis reveals that, under constant rates, these sequences act similarly to random walks, with parity symmetry ensuring an even number of photons never occurs. Conversely, dynamically changing rates produce distinct, non-ergodic temporal signatures in the emission process. Specifically, third-state quantum dots can generate non-classical, anti-correlated light, while three-state systems, despite their ability to emit pairs of photons, do not display anti-bunching properties.

We introduce a new analytical equation of state (EOS) designed for pure alkali metals, built upon a non-extensive entropy formalism and tailored to their specific quantum characteristics. This model offers a versatile framework capable of generating an $EOS$ across diverse thermodynamic conditions, quantum regimes, and states involving pressure, volume, and temperature. From this proposed $EOS$, we derive key thermodynamic properties, including internal energy, heat capacity, entropy, and compressibility. Our calculated heat capacity and entropy align well with available experimental data and existing theoretical models. Notably, our analysis of the internal energy reveals a distinct quantum effect: it exhibits a non-monotonic behavior with respect to volume, contrasting sharply with the monotonic trends observed in both classical and standard quantum descriptions.

The vector-vector correlation function is used to investigate vector meson mass spectra under conditions of local vector and axial-vector chemical potentials. By employing an effective Lagrangian for light vector mesons within the framework of QCD sum rules, we analyze how a chiral imbalance influences both the masses of light vector mesons and their relevant QCD matrix elements.

This paper introduces a distributed algorithm designed to establish a shared view among nodes in a network facing communication delays and the presence of Byzantine nodes. The algorithm operates within a synchronous environment where message transmission between any two nodes is guaranteed within a known upper bound of $\Delta$ time units. It assumes a network topology that is initially unknown to the nodes but synchronous, with at most $f < n/3$ Byzantine nodes out of a total of $n$. The proposed solution is both view-consistent and -valid while offering optimality in terms of synchrony requirements, time complexity, and the limit on tolerated faulty nodes.

In numerical relativity simulations involving complex, non-axisymmetric initial data with multiple moving singularities, analytically solving the Hamiltonian constraint is often unfeasible. To address this, we developed a new method for the conformal time-spatial decomposition (TSD) of the constraint that allows for an iterative resolution using finite difference techniques. This approach treats the method as a system of elliptic equations where the Newton-Raphson algorithm is employed for its solution. We validate this algorithm by successfully solving the constraint for two distinct configurations: a binary black hole system and a system featuring a rotating neutron star surrounded by an accretion disk.

The primary objective of the JUNO experiment is to detect neutrinos arising from a nearby nuclear fusion facility to investigate neutrino oscillations, specifically the squared mass difference squared $| \Delta m^2_{32} |$ with high precision. The proposed detector comprises a vast 20-kiloton liquid scintillator sphere situated 60 kilometers from the source, engineered to capture approximately $10^4$ elastic $\bar{\nu}_e$-p interactions per year. These events are characterized by a mean energy of 3.9 MeV and a 10% relative energy resolution, allowing neutrino energy reconstruction to be resolved with an accuracy of 30 keV. The analysis of pulse shape waveforms enables the effective suppression of backgrounds to levels below 0.1 events/year, ensuring a clean signal environment.

Long sequence time-series forecasting plays a vital role in diverse fields, including weather prediction, traffic analysis, and health monitoring. Although recent deep learning advancements have significantly enhanced forecasting accuracy, existing methods often struggle with excessive computational costs when processing long historical sequences. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel framework for long-term forecasting that leverages pre-trained language models pre-adapted to temporal series data. Our approach utilizes these models to compress both the forecasting task and historical data, thereby significantly enhancing prediction performance while maintaining efficiency.

This study introduces the initial atmospheric dispersion measurements derived from an Atmospheric Dispersion Corrector (ADC) integrated with the Very Large Telescope's Unit Telesciles (UTs). The research analyzes data from the UTT-ADC configuration, which was employed to monitor the double star 6 Aquilae. The observational results indicate that the primary atmospheric dispersion correction is achieved by applying symmetrical, opposite prism pairs to the beam. The study details the calibration process for the ADC, the determination of the sky's atmospheric dispersion profile, and the quantification of the precision achievable with this setup.

This study introduces a novel approach to ranker training utilizing knowledge distillation. Our proposal involves generating pseudo labels for query-document pairs via a teacher model, which are subsequently used to supervise the student model. While prior research in this domain has primarily relied on log-probabilities as the source of knowledge, we demonstrate that incorporating additional soft knowledge derived from the teacher model's output vectors significantly enhances performance. Experiments conducted on industry-standard datasets confirm our method's effectiveness, achieving notable improvements over baseline techniques.

Ultralight bosonic dark matter (DM) interacts weakly with ordinary matter, causing minute oscillations in mass and energy density at extremely low frequencies (near zero). These fluctuations can be measured using high-precision, ultra-sensitive gravimetric sensors to identify the properties of ultralight DM. In this study, we examine how classical and quantum noise impacts the detection of these DM signals through gravimetry. We demonstrate that the most effective strategy for identifying ultralight DM signals involves analyzing data near the classical noise floor at nearly zero frequency. To achieve this classical noise limit at low frequencies, the system must exhibit a flat or rising noise profile there, a requirement that necessitates minimizing the noise contribution from the suspension system. Conversely, to extend the DM parameter space accessible to these experiments, operating beyond the quantum noise limit is essential. We evaluate various quantum gravimetric detection schemes, including optomechanical dark matter detectors. Our findings indicate that current and near-future classical dark matter experiments can constrain certain classes of ultralight DM particles, whereas future quantum gravimetric experiments have the potential to probe a significantly broader range of ultralight DM parameter space.

This study investigates a class of nonlinear, ill-posed inverse problems aimed at determining $\mu$, a Radon measure on $\mathbb{R}^d$, from the $k$ Fourier coefficients corresponding to the first $k$ lowest frequencies. The data provided takes the form of the $j$-th coefficient, $u_j$, which is computed as $\int \phi_j(x) \exp(\mu(x)) \, d x$, where $\{\phi_j\}$ represents a known basis for a specific function space. The analysis demonstrates uniqueness of the solution $\mu$ within a metric geometry defined by the metric entropy of $\mu$ when the available low-frequency data is sufficiently precise. Furthermore, the paper establishes Holder-type stability estimates under the condition that higher-frequency coefficients are also accessed. The P4 language enables the definition of programmable packet processing for modern network devices, such as programmable switches. Although the community has established various P4 compilers, no official semantic analyzer exists. Consequently, various runtime errors can occur despite successful compilation, as these tools prioritize generating machine code over error detection. This paper introduces the P4 semantic analyzer written in Rust, developed using an recursive descent approach to verify P4 programs for syntax and logical errors. All identified errors are reported with precise line and column references. Evaluations demonstrate that analyzing a program using this Rust implementation incurs negligible overhead compared to running existing P4 compilers.

In finite element methods for fluid dynamics, vector and tensor calculations frequently demand a transport step. This paper introduces a novel approach to solving the transport equation by representing transported fields within a higher-order function space than the base velocity field. Although this increases computational cost per step, it enhances overall algorithmic convergence. We examine this method using transport equations from both incompressible and compressible fluid dynamics.

Deep learning has become a primary driver of recent breakthroughs in computer vision, natural language processing, and audio analysis. Despite this success, its ethical implications, particularly regarding automated decision-making, have drawn significant attention. This paper offers a concise overview of key ethical challenges within deep learning, including bias, transparency, data privacy, and the potential for misuse. Following this overview, we examine specific strategies for mitigating these risks, with a focused analysis on reducing model bias through methods like fair regularization, post-processing adjustments, and training with diverse datasets.

Recent advancements have introduced an efficient class of Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Runge-Kutta Methods (HRKMs), distinguished by their ability to preserve the energy of the continuous Hamiltonian functional when exact quadrature is employed. These methods integrate seamlessly with Boundary Value Methods (BVMs)—a category of time-stepping technique renowned for simultaneously achieving high order of accuracy and excellent long-term stability. By combining these traits, HRKKM-based BVMs (KM-BVMs) conserve the discrete energy of Hamiltonian systems throughout simulations. This paper establishes that KM-BVMs possess the A-stability required for solving Ordinary Differential Equates (ODEs) and demonstrates their superior efficiency over conventional collocation-based Runge-Kutta methods. Specifically, for approximating solutions to the 1D Schr\"odinger equation, KM-BVMs attain the same computational cost as traditional approaches while delivering markedly enhanced accuracy.

This paper introduces a novel multi-agent reinforcement learning approach for training deep neural networks, designed to overcome the diminishing gradient issue. Our method employs a multi-layer critic architecture alongside specific actor and critic roles. Actor networks manage policy updates at the layer group level, while local critics assess the value of these individual layer groups. Additionally, a dedicated network refines policy decisions based on feedback from the local critics. Experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that this model achieves superior performance compared to existing methods, with results supporting the hypothesis that performing reinforcement learning on a coarse granularity helps mitigate vanishing gradients during deep learning.
